items.title: Are AI-Made Reservations Fair?
items.author: Sam Stone
items.summary: Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the end of ‘Chicken Shop
items.text:
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the end of ‘Chicken Shop Date.’

Welcome back to Open Tab. Labor Day weekend was excuse enough for me to make salmon tacos with pineapple-chile salsa—always a hit—followed by a fluffy, aromatic olive oil cake. I’ve found myself cooking at home almost exclusively in recent weeks, but, in no particular order, here are the New York Restaurants I’ve been meaning to hit: Dean’s, Hommali, Kirbee’s, Graciela, and El Califa de Leon. Make of that list what you will.

This week marks 25 years since the attacks on 9/11—many in the food world are remembering Windows on the World, the restaurant opened on the top floors of the North Tower. CNN also released a documentary on the restaurant, which was at one time the highest-grossing standalone restaurant in the country.

Another fascinating read: Ruby Tandoh in the New Yorker on Saudi Arabia’s quest to rebrand as a culinary capital which includes, among other things, the introduction of Michelin stars last year. Michelin has been evaluating more and more cities, often partnering with (read: getting paid by) local tourism boards who recognize that the distinction can attract a real wave of tourists to the area. But when I interviewed him a couple years ago, Gwendal Poullennec, international director of the Michelin Guide, insisted that the guide’s expansion wasn’t about the money—it was about finding more cities with “culinary potential” than ever before.

Oh, also they’re doing $60 loaves of rye bread now. Oy.

Also in this week’s Open Tab: the people using AI agents to score reservations, what exactly are ultraprocessed foods?, and the eternal question: Is it ever ok to bring your own seasonings to restaurants?

AI agents? I have reservations

This week’s addition to the AI hellscape? Personal AI agents. Meta released Muse, and Instinct continues to gain traction. These are agents that can respond to emails, book plane tickets, secure you a spot in a workout class, arrange and rearrange your calendar, and, yes, make grab that impossible-to-get dinner reservation. Hypothetically.

Using AI agents to nab tough reservations may also get you banned from reservation platforms, as one user found out this week. The way these agents work is by spamming the reservation platform hundreds of times per hour for hours on end. The reservation platforms flag that as suspicious activity, and may ban your account.

When I reached out to Resy for comment, a spokesperson clarified that the company doesn’t permit “unapproved third-party bots or AI agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform.” That’s not to say the company is anti-AI—it’s recently announced integrations with ChatGPT and Claude. But rather, it says, Resy wants to maintain a “fair reservation experience for diners.”

And that’s really the crux of the issue; it’s not hard to imagine a day in the not-too-distant future when AI agents can work within a platform's terms of service (in fact, that day may have actually been earlier this week) grabbing the toughest tables the second they become available. It’s an undeniable upping of the ante in the already impossible reservations war. What are non-agent-assisted restaurant lovers to do? How can restaurants, many dependent on these platforms to stay booked, respond? Is this the beginning of a golden age for walk-in only spots?

What exactly makes a food ultraprocessed?

This week, California approved a landmark bill that establishes a process for which foods may label themselves as non-ultraprocessed. This comes after the state was the first in the nation to put forth a solid definition of what exactly an ultraprocessed food is. Although there’s been a lot of talk about ultraprocessed foods (or UPFs)—mostly stemming from the MAHA movement—there’s not a true consensus on how to delineate which foods are ultraprocessed and which aren’t.

I mean, sure, maybe you simply know it when you see it: an apple is not ultraprocessed. Gently glowing, fire-engine red flamin’ hot cheetos boxed mac and cheese is ultraprocessed.

At the federal level, the US is still in the process of drawing up an official definition, but around the world, several definitions are held as true. Brazilian researchers define UPFs as all foods with industrial ingredients like sweeteners or emulsifiers. Research group Healthy Eating Research says they’re foods “processed to the extent that they are no longer recognizable as their original plant/animal source.”

Though there isn’t a firm categorization (yet), we’re already beginning to see colossal food companies respond to the discourse. PepsiCo is reportedly shifting focus to fresh foods instead of processed ones, and some cereal companies have stopped using artificial dyes. All good stuff, but I will say this: You can pry my flamin’ hot cheetos mac and cheese out of my cold, dead, cholesterol-clogged hands.

Some people bring their own birthday cakes to restaurants. Others bring their own bottle of wine to enjoy with dinner. And then there are the people who bring their own seasonings to restaurants. It’s a controversial topic, but for those who don’t leave the house without their pocket Maldon, their Calabrian chili oil, their fancy olive oil it’s really no question at all. Read Maggie Hennessy’s intriguing piece on Bon Appétit for more.

items.title: How Much You Need to Exercise for Better Sleep, According to Experts
items.author: Dean Stattmann
items.summary: Ever notice how some workouts put you to sleep while others make you feel like someone switched out your vitamins for caffeine pills? You’re not going crazy.
items.text:
Ever notice how some workouts put you to sleep while others make you feel like someone switched out your vitamins for caffeine pills? You’re not going crazy. Exercise can significantly impact your sleep—for better or for worse—depending on how, and when, you work out.

Unfortunately, the exercise-sleep relationship is not as straightforward as the internet’s sleepmaxxers might lead you to believe. While research has unlocked some valuable insights that you can start putting into practice later tonight, there’s still a lot we don’t know. "Part of what's vexing about this is we don't have the mechanism totally locked down,” says James Wyatt, PhD, clinical sleep disorder specialist at Rush University System for Health in Chicago.

"It's also important to caveat that, while the data is enormously helpful, there's so much intra-individual variability,” says Kristen Holmes, PhD, global head of human performance and principal scientist at Whoop. At the end of the day (literally), sleep is a complex chemical equation that differs to various degrees from person to person.

But back to those valuable insights. From morning HIIT workouts that reset your circadian rhythm to an evening workout to hack your body’s natural cooling system, here are some of the best ways to use exercise to fall asleep faster, according to experts.

Working out in general won’t make you fall asleep faster

Exercise can certainly reduce the time it takes to fall asleep, but not for the reason that many wellness influencers would have you think—that is, by spurring your body’s natural production of adenosine, a sleep-inducing compound that is also a byproduct of exercise.

Your body’s cells rely on a molecule called adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, for energy. It’s a universal fuel source that powers everything from muscle contractions to brain function to simply existing. As ATP is utilized, it produces a compound called adenosine. Adenosine is not a waste product. In fact, it is highly valuable. “In muscle, adenosine helps to reduce inflammation and limit damage during periods of metabolic stress,” says Dr. Holmes. Meanwhile, in the brain, adenosine accumulates throughout the day, gradually making you feel sleepier. “In sleep science, this is called ‘sleep pressure,’” says Dr. Holmes.

So it seems perfectly plausible that the key to falling asleep faster would simply be to exercise. More exertion equals more adenosine and therefore greater sleep pressure. A 2007 study published in the journal Neuroscience actually found that when rats engaged in intense exercise, the levels of adenosine in their brains increased significantly.

But that’s not how it works in humans. "Adenosine can do an awful lot of different things in the brain and in the body, but we have to separate these,” says Dr. Wyatt. This is because adenosine doesn’t cross the blood-brain barrier—the wrapping around your brain that selectively allows certain chemicals in and not others. “If you build up adenosine in your body as a byproduct of exercising, that will not influence what happens in your brain,” Dr. Wyatt says. “That adenosine doesn't make it into the brain.”

Make no mistake, adenosine is still crucial for sleep in humans. "Adenosine on its own is one of the major chemicals that helps us fall asleep at night and get deep sleep for the first couple of hours,” Dr. Wyatt says. But only adenosine that is created in the brain will ultimately contribute to increasing sleep pressure.

The timing of your workout may be more important than the intensity

In terms of how hard or you need to work out in order to fall asleep faster, experts aren’t entirely sure of this, or if it even matters all that much. "We don't have a lot of great data on the intensity of exercise that's needed,” says Dr. Wyatt. The main reason for this, it seems, is that exercise’s ability to improve sleep is likely not a direct function of intensity—or any single factor, for that matter—but rather a combination of variables, including timing. For example, working out at a high intensity could be helpful in the morning, but detrimental later on in the day.

"One way that exercise could indirectly influence sleep is that it strengthens your circadian rhythm—that 24-hour daily rhythm of alertness during the day and sleepiness at night,” says Dr. Wyatt. In other words, working out earlier in the day can help your body understand that it’s daytime, and that in a couple of hours it will be time to sleep. But slow cardio isn’t going to cut it. “In animals, if you look at a rat or a mouse, the time during the day when you give them access to exercise dramatically shifts their circadian rhythm,” Dr. Wyatt says. “But in humans, exercise is a very weak signal for aligning ourselves to the 24-hour day, so it has to be an awful lot of exercise to have a notable effect.” (We recommend giving this HIIT workout a try.)

As for going all out in the evening, in a 2025 study published in the journal Nature Communications, researchers observed that high-strain workouts done within four hours of bedtime had a range of detrimental effects on sleep. In the study, data from nearly 15,000 Whoop members across more than four million nights revealed that an intense evening workout can delay sleep onset, reduce total sleep duration, and degrade overall sleep quality. “Basically, what we found is that intense exercise ending within four hours of going to bed was associated with these changes in sleep,” says Dr. Holmes. “When you're exercising at a high intensity, you're releasing adrenaline, cortisol, and epinephrine, so it's going to take time afterwards for that to dissipate.”

How to work out to fall asleep faster

According to Dr. Wyatt and Dr. Holmes, there are basically two types of workouts that may potentially help you fall asleep faster. The first one, as mentioned, is a high-intensity session during the day—the earlier the better—to help click your circadian rhythm into sync with the day. Ideally, you’ll want to also include some natural sunlight in the equation or, better yet, train outdoors. “From a circadian perspective, you want to create as much contrast between the day and the night as possible,” says Dr. Holmes.

The other option is an evening workout—albeit a relatively light one. According to the Whoop study data, when people engaged in a low-intensity evening workout, they experienced better sleep quality than those who didn’t exercise at all—and they only needed one hour of buffer time between training and going to bed.

The sleep-inducing power of a low-intensity evening workout has nothing to do with your circadian rhythm and everything to do with body temperature. As you approach bedtime, your body is naturally configured to move heat away from its core—a process that contributes to feelings of sleepiness. Exercise, of course, does the opposite and raises your core temperature, but it also makes your body work harder to lower it. According to John Hopkins Medicine, core temperature starts to fall about 30–90 minutes after exercising. Timing your workout to end 1–2 hours before bedtime—which, according to Dr. Wyatt, also happens to be right around the time your brain starts releasing melatonin—effectively layers that post-workout temperature drop on top of your body’s natural cooling process, creating the perfect sleep storm. “Exercise ramps up body temperature even more, and therefore it has an even steeper drop,” Dr. Wyatt says. “The steepness of that drop in body temperature is what might be associated with the ability to fall asleep faster.”

“The general guidance is: Evening exercise can help sleep, too close to bed is bad, and too far away from bedtime may be ineffective. But again, there are those individual differences,” Dr. Wyatt says. “This is why it's challenging. It's not going to be just a single recipe that says, ‘Okay, do this one thing and sleep suddenly gets better.’ You have to find the combination that works for you.”

items.title: Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
items.summary: During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home,
items.text:
During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home, with the presentation of his photographic data to locals who are already putting it to work to bring these traditions back to life.

Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests

Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.

Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.

The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.

The altar for worshipping Shōgatsu-sama on the first day of the new year. (© Haga Hideo)

A ceremony to pray for a good harvest, performed after a paddy dried out during winter has been worked with a hoe in preparation for planting. (© Haga Hideo)

Preparing mochibana, bits of mochi pounded rice threaded onto branches, as a stand-in for Shōgatsu-sama, on January 13. (© Haga Hideo)

A divination ritual conducted on the evening of January 14. Twelve soybeans are roasted in the irori sunken hearth and used to predict the weather for the coming year according to the degree of charring. (© Haga Hideo)

Torigoya is conducted even today on koshōgatsu, January 15. Bamboo, straw, and New Year decorations are burned to return Shōgatsu-sama to the heavens. (© Haga Hideo)

Warmed by hearty oden stew, children gather in a hut to sing a song to drive away birds, which eat the grain the fields, in the hope of an abundant harvest. (© Haga Hideo)

Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki

In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.

For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.

As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.

Iwaki, where Haga got his start as a folklore photographer, is today on the verge of losing its traditional farming culture. The Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing, which opened in 1999, is leading efforts to preserve what is left of those traditions. The museum collects and displays all manner of artifacts related to local life.

Five traditional thatched-roof houses, dismantled and transported from various parts of Iwaki, have been re-erected in the museum’s vast grounds. Meticulously preserved, they reproduce a premodern farm village. On display inside the houses are farming tools of the era; visitors can also try their hand at working in the fields and paddies outside. Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.

Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests

Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.

Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.

The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.

Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki

In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.

For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.

As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.

Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.

items.title: Saloons, school and specialty coffee: NWSL players enjoy new era of side hustles
items.author: Roey Hadar
items.summary: On a cold winter night in Ketchum, Idaho, Chicago Stars midfielder Bea Franklin was pulling off a different sort of physical feat than what she usually does on
items.text:
On a cold winter night in Ketchum, Idaho, Chicago Stars midfielder Bea Franklin was pulling off a different sort of physical feat than what she usually does on the soccer field. Under the eyes of taxidermied animals at the Pioneer Saloon, she deftly balanced martinis as a cocktail waitress, wearing cowgirl boots and ensuring the olives didn’t drip when she walked down stairs.

Franklin did not take a second job as a cocktail waitress in a Rocky Mountain ski resort town not out of necessity, but as a way to think about more than just the sport that has dominated much of her life.

“It was just so much fun, and a really great way to kind of disconnect from soccer,” Franklin said.

Hardly half a decade ago, a player like Franklin, a 25-year-old in her third pro season, might have needed a job like this just to get by.

Five years ago this summer, NWSL players organized the “No More Side Hustles” campaign to highlight the league’s low pay and the need for players to get second jobs while playing, training and working as full-time professional athletes.

At the time, a third of the NWSL Players Association’s members made the league minimum salary of $22,000; 75% made $31,000 or less. Jessica McDonald, a World Cup winner, worked at Amazon packing boxes for 10 hours a day while running training sessions for young players at night. Kristen Hamilton, a three-time league champion, drove for DoorDash. Others cleaned homes, worked as receptionists or mopped floors.

It spoke to a major problem that the league has, by and large, addressed successfully. The NWSLPA agreed to its first collective bargaining agreement with the league in 2022. Under the current CBA, reached in 2024, the minimum salary for players is $50,500 for the 2026 season – nearly the same amount as the maximum in 2021 ($52,500).

Now, with the security of a living wage, players are free to take on academic, professional and entrepreneurial pursuits. Not because they have to, but because they want to.

Washington Spirit defender Gabrielle Carle is working on becoming a doctor after her playing career wraps. She said she briefly considered doing both until realizing that was too ambitious, even for her.

“I was like, ‘Oh, this is gonna be complicated,’” Carle said. “These two don’t really work together.”

Nevertheless, Carle was not deterred. During the 2025 season, a career year for the full-back from Quebec, she studied during the season for the MCAT and then took the exam in January. The 27-year-old said she passed the score she hoped to reach and plans to take advantage of the three-year window to use the score in a medical school application.

“I’m going to be 30 years old. I can decide if that’s a good time for me to retire or if I want to keep going. But if I do decide to move on with my career and retire from soccer, then I have that score and I can immediately move on to the next part of my life,” Carle said.

Even with a few years between a decision about medical school, Carle has relished the chance to do more than just play soccer and keep herself in what she dubbed her “smart mode”. She is applying for positions where she can conduct sports medicine research.

Carle is not the only player to juggle scouting reports with schoolbooks. Her Washington Spirit teammate, Lucia Di Guglielmo, has a master’s degree in industrial chemistry. In England, Chelsea captain Erin Cuthbert has earned her MBA, while Manchester United goalkeeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce put her degree in marine biology to use by hosting students for workshops at a local zoo.

This year, the NWSL and Syracuse University launched a partnership that allows players to pursue online degrees and certificates in programs ranging from sports analytics and cybersecurity to business management and accounting.

Franklin, who studied finance at the University of Arkansas, took a job last season at Bank of America as a wealth management analyst on afternoons after training and on her off days and helping manage the investments of some extremely wealthy clients. She felt that the skills she learned are helpful for someone like her, even if, as she readily concedes, she does not fall into that income bracket.

“It puts some real-world application into how people get credit and actually going through banking process or, even just seeing the nitty-gritty of opening a bank account on the other side,” Franklin said. “And now, when I do it again, I’ll have a bit more patience for the person on the other end of the phone, because that was me sometimes.”

Several players have gone further by starting businesses of their own. This summer, two NWSL players on the Canadian national team launched businesses: Chicago forward Jordyn Huitema started Jordyskin, a skincare line, and Denver Summit full-back Janine Sonis created 90Brew, a specialty coffee brand.

Coffee has been a frequent jumping-off point for soccer players looking to go entrepreneurial: Cuthbert has a coffee brand called Ruby Alba; England legend Jill Scott created Boxx2Boxx coffee shop in Manchester; and a group of Kansas City Current teammates opened Pitchside Coffee.

Sonis launched her business in the middle of a career year on the field, where she has scored nine goals for the Summit in their expansion season.

Earlier this month, 90Brew started taking its first orders. Sonis said it was part of a tumultuous 18-month process tied to a lingering problem early in her pro soccer career.

“I actually started drinking coffee because, funny enough, I couldn’t stay awake,” Sonis said.

A self-described coffee fanatic, Sonis followed the lead of her husband Ethan, who launched an athletic training business in 2018. A joking conversation with a friend after the 2024 season became serious when her husband asked her why she would not just go for it and start the business.

Sonis was quick to credit the support network she has had in starting the business. In a turn from the days when teams were indifferent or even hostile to players in the years before the league instituted major reforms, she said that her club has been immensely supportive. It doesn’t hurt that, independently of each other, the Summit and 90Brew share similar shades of green.

“We picked those colors before the logo for the Summit had come out, which is really funny and just really kind of validated what we were doing,” she said. “I remember the moment that the logo came out for the Summit and I’m like, ‘You’ve gotta be kidding me.’”

The 32-year-old Sonis is a full decade removed from her NWSL debut. She knew the darker days of side hustles and second jobs. For her, it is a full-circle moment, and a sign of just how far the league has come.

“Even really not that far in the past, which is crazy that people had to have two jobs and their NWSL salaries weren’t supporting them enough not to have to do something else,” she said. “And now here I am being able to support myself in multiple ventures because of the direction that the game has moved in.”

Under the current CBA, reached in 2024, the minimum salary for players is $50,500 for the 2026 season – nearly the same amount as the maximum in 2021 ($52,500).
Now, with the security of a living wage, players are free to take on academic, professional and entrepreneurial pursuits. Not because they have to, but because they want to.

Washington Spirit defender Gabrielle Carle is working on becoming a doctor after her playing career wraps. She said she briefly considered doing both until realizing that was too ambitious, even for her.
“I was like, ‘Oh, this is gonna be complicated,’” Carle said. “These two don’t really work together.”

blocks.c: Gabrielle Carle dribbles during a Washington Spirit game.

blocks.x: Nevertheless, Carle was not deterred. During the 2025 season, a career year for the full-back from Quebec, she studied during the season for the MCAT and then took the exam in January. The 27-year-old said she passed the score she hoped to reach and plans to take advantage of the three-year window to use the score in a medical school application.

“I’m going to be 30 years old. I can decide if that’s a good time for me to retire or if I want to keep going. But if I do decide to move on with my career and retire from soccer, then I have that score and I can immediately move on to the next part of my life,” Carle said.

Even with a few years between a decision about medical school, Carle has relished the chance to do more than just play soccer and keep herself in what she dubbed her “smart mode”. She is applying for positions where she can conduct sports medicine research.

Carle is not the only player to juggle scouting reports with schoolbooks. Her Washington Spirit teammate, Lucia Di Guglielmo, has a master’s degree in industrial chemistry. In England, Chelsea captain Erin Cuthbert has earned her MBA, while Manchester United goalkeeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce put her degree in marine biology to use by hosting students for workshops at a local zoo.

This year, the NWSL and Syracuse University launched a partnership that allows players to pursue online degrees and certificates in programs ranging from sports analytics and cybersecurity to business management and accounting.

Franklin, who studied finance at the University of Arkansas, took a job last season at Bank of America as a wealth management analyst on afternoons after training and on her off days and helping manage the investments of some extremely wealthy clients. She felt that the skills she learned are helpful for someone like her, even if, as she readily concedes, she does not fall into that income bracket.

Several players have gone further by starting businesses of their own. This summer, two NWSL players on the Canadian national team launched businesses: Chicago forward Jordyn Huitema started Jordyskin, a skincare line, and Denver Summit full-back Janine Sonis created 90Brew, a specialty coffee brand.

Coffee has been a frequent jumping-off point for soccer players looking to go entrepreneurial: Cuthbert has a coffee brand called Ruby Alba; England legend Jill Scott created Boxx2Boxx coffee shop in Manchester; and a group of Kansas City Current teammates opened Pitchside Coffee.
Sonis launched her business in the middle of a career year on the field, where she has scored nine goals for the Summit in their expansion season.
Earlier this month, 90Brew started taking its first orders. Sonis said it was part of a tumultuous 18-month process tied to a lingering problem early in her pro soccer career.
“I actually started drinking coffee because, funny enough, I couldn’t stay awake,” Sonis said.

A self-described coffee fanatic, Sonis followed the lead of her husband Ethan, who launched an athletic training business in 2018. A joking conversation with a friend after the 2024 season became serious when her husband asked her why she would not just go for it and start the business.

Sonis was quick to credit the support network she has had in starting the business. In a turn from the days when teams were indifferent or even hostile to players in the years before the league instituted major reforms, she said that her club has been immensely supportive. It doesn’t hurt that, independently of each other, the Summit and 90Brew share similar shades of green.

“We picked those colors before the logo for the Summit had come out, which is really funny and just really kind of validated what we were doing,” she said. “I remember the moment that the logo came out for the Summit and I’m like, ‘You’ve gotta be kidding me.’”

The 32-year-old Sonis is a full decade removed from her NWSL debut. She knew the darker days of side hustles and second jobs. For her, it is a full-circle moment, and a sign of just how far the league has come.

“Even really not that far in the past, which is crazy that people had to have two jobs and their NWSL salaries weren’t supporting them enough not to have to do something else,” she said. “And now here I am being able to support myself in multiple ventures because of the direction that the game has moved in.”

items.title: Champions League review: Irish heroics, rejected resignations and Mourinho’s return
items.author: John Brewin
items.summary:
A big week for

The league phase has been previewed as Barcelona’s first step toward reclaiming a crown last lifted in 2015, with disappointments aplenty
items.text:
A big week for

The league phase has been previewed as Barcelona’s first step toward reclaiming a crown last lifted in 2015, with disappointments aplenty since. Lionel Messi claiming just one Champions League title in the last decade of his time at Camp Nou is the starkest statistic. The player anointed as Messi’s successor, Lamine Yamal, is already a European and world champion for Spain, so this is the next frontier. A soggy Wednesday evening at Camp Nou saw Hansi Flick’s team show their attacking chops remain of the highest quality in a 5-1 defeat of Feyenoord. The club presidential regime of Joan Laporta continues to pull levers to confound financial experts, with Gabriel Jesus, one of the summer’s arrivals, scoring his first Barca goal. Yamal got on the scoresheet via a scruffy free-kick after Raphinha had reminded there are further dimensions to that all-star attack, his first goal of his pair two sending Feyenoord defenders skidding.

Until Troy Parrott headed to Seville this summer, the chances of Real Betis v Lille being a leading attraction to the Irish diaspora were minimal. But now the team in green and white have become an Irish obsession. The goalscorer in their World Cup playoff win in Hungary last year is approaching national hero status. Opting for Andalusia instead of leading West Ham in the Championship confirmed him as a player with broad horizons; the former Tottenham trainee is hitting the heights in La Liga. Having scored the winner against Real Madrid last weekend, throwing back to José Mourinho his rejection when a Spurs teenager, he delivered again in northern France. His dragged, left-footed finish grabbed a 3-2 lead Betis successfully held. “I don’t think I’ll ever have a better night in my whole life,” Parrott said of his glory night in Budapest. If that still holds true, his Friday and Tuesday will have gone close to emulating it.

Weird scenes after Fenerbahce’s 1-1 draw with Roma when Ismail Kartal, the Turkish club’s veteran coach, resigned post-match “to clear the way”. The drama was heightened when the Fenerbahce president, Aziz Yildirim, said he would not be accepting the resignation. “There’s no need for him ‌to say that he’d continue,” Yildirim said. “I am his senior, I told him to continue and that’s it. We are a family.” The explanation given for such a sudden exit was Kartal’s annoyance at a bottle being lobbed in his direction. Watch this space.

Player of the week

Ballon D’Or season is upon us, and a leading nominee must be Bayern’s brilliant Michael Olise, who scored two goals against Bodø/Glimt. The Norwegians attempted to aggressively mark him but were left with twisted blood as his team scored five second-half goals. The Frenchman gave a typically dry post-match interview. Asked how it feels to score great goals, he said: “I don’t know … I just shoot and it goes in.”

Club in focus

Manchester United on Thursday faced a club formed in 2017, three years after Luke Shaw, who missed the game, was signed. Sabah, Azerbaijan’s champions last season, breaking the dominance of Qurban Qurbanov’s Qarabag, are coached by Valdas Dambrauskas, a former United soccer schools and Brentford youth coach who also worked as a pub cleaner and gardener in the UK. His journey from Lithuania to Manchester was funded by a win on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, where he walked away from Vilnius’s equivalent of Regis Philbin with a sum commensurate with a year’s salary. The homecoming was not too happy as United were ready 4-0 winners, Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes in particular turning on the style. “He absolutely destroyed us,” Dambrauskas said of Fernandes. That did not bode well for Sabah’s matches ahead: Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli travel to Azerbaijan, while a trip to Arsenal awaits.

They said it

“There’s a lot of criticism when a match is boring, but it was crazy today. . … It could easily have ended 7-6. Our midfield was weak, they made changes very early, and I didn’t have much to work with in the centre of the pitch. … I agree with Raul that the goals came as a result of their errors.” José Mourinho’s Real Madrid return is already under scrutiny, and before being interviewed on Movistar after a close-run 2-1 defeat of Inter, he had to listen to on-air criticism from Raúl González, a Madrileno legend. Those midfield comments appeared directed at Trent Alexander-Arnold, who played as one of the trio on a night where fans at the Santiago Bernabéu made clear that better is expected.

skip past newsletter promotion

Looking ahead

The other side of an elongated international break, the wait will be long – more than a month – for the second round of matches. Holders Paris Saint-Germain, looking for their third straight title, travelling to Manchester City is the grand-slam fixture. Enzo Maresca has made a decent fist of succeeding Pep Guardiola, with four wins in four. Erling Haaland’s pair of goals at Porto took him to 167, third on his club’s all-time scorers’ list, 10 behind Eric Brook, who played his last game during the second world war.

Mourinho, should he remain in charge at Real Madrid, will return to Roma while Manchester United travel to Atlético Madrid, who knocked out United in the last 16 in 2021-22, their only previous meeting in the competition.

items.title: Ballon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turning
items.author: Jacob Steinberg
items.summary: Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and
items.text:
Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.

The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.

As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.

“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”

The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.

Now comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.

Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.

Graphic showing Premier League games have been more end-to-end early in 2026‑27

There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up. Manchester City may soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.

Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals – Arsenal taking on Chelsea at the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.

Havertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard, Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.

This matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.

The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.

items.text:
Saturday

Golf

6.40am (all times BST)Solheim Cup live

The 20th edition of the Solheim Cup is under way, and for the first time in the Netherlands. Angela Stanford’s Americans are the slight favourites and defending champions, but they have not won on European soil since Germany in 2015. The US, as holders, need only 14 of the 28 points available to retain the crystal trophy. Scott Murray and Matt Cooper offer live coverage of day two’s foursomes (6.40am) and fourballs (12.05am), with Ewan Murray reporting from Bernardus Golf.

Football

8amMatchday live

Join Tom Bassam for the latest news and buildup to Saturday’s football action. We will keep pace with all the day’s breaking news from around the grounds for seven Premier League matches, plus a full Championship and EFL programme. Join our Matchday live community by sending your thoughts and queries to matchday.live@theguardian.com.

Premier League

3pmClockwatch

Barry Glendenning keeps watch over all five 3pm kick-offs in the Premier League, and will be focusing on two of the afternoon’s most compelling games. Liverpool’s season took ⁠a while to get going under Andoni Iraola but after wins at Ipswich and then Atlético Madrid in the Champions League they will relish another home clash against a Fulham side managed by the former Liverpool player Álvaro Arbeloa. After three successive defeats and seven goals conceded, Arbeloa is already feeling the pressure of management in the top flight. Alongside last season’s top two, only promoted Hull remain unbeaten but their brilliant start faces an acid test against Xabi Alonso’s free-scoring Chelsea.

Formula One

3pmSpanish Grand Prix qualifying live

Kimi Antonelli is Formula One’s man of the moment but Mercedes’ 20-year-old championship leader faces a Monumental challenge in Spain this weekend, along with all his rivals. Fresh from ⁠becoming the first Italian since ⁠1966 to win his home race at Monza, Antonelli will be entering new territory when the Spanish capital’s Madring makes its grand prix debut with its signature La Monumental. The banked curve is a 550m-long high-speed 270-degree bend with a crest on the exit meaning drivers momentarily take it blind as they look up at the sky. Mercedes, winners of nine ‌of the first 13 races, should be in the mix but can expect a tougher fight than Monza, where they finished one-two, putting Antonelli 66 points clear of ‌his teammate George Russell. We will have lap-by-lap coverage of qualifying from Philip Cornwall, and Giles Richards reporting from Madrid.

Premier League

5.30pmTottenham v Everton live

Despite a £300m close-season splurge, Roberto De Zerbi’s Spurs are winless in their first three games and without a goal. Little more than three months ago, the Italian completed his Tottenham rescue mission as they beat Everton on the final day of the season to secure their top-flight status. On Saturday, David Moyes’ Everton are the visitors again and, while the stakes are not so high, De Zerbi desperately needs a victory to instil some belief that the money has been well spent. There will be a live blog of the match, with David Hytner reporting from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Tennis

7pmUS Open women’s singles final

Elena Rybakina rallied to beat Coco Gauff in a thrilling semi-final to earn a title showdown with the defending champion, Aryna Sabalenka, and take a step towards her third grand slam crown. The pair have met in two previous slam finals, with Sabalenka defeating Rybakina in the 2023 Australian Open decider before the second seed ​levelled the score at Melbourne Park in ‌January. Sabalenka, who will lose her world No 1 status to her opponent on Monday regardless of the result, is seeking to join Chris Evert and Serena Williams as the only women to win three straight US Open titles. Katy Murrells helms the live blog, with Tumaini Carayol reporting from Flushing Meadows.

Premier League

8pmSunderland v Arsenal live

Stability has been the order of the day at Arsenal, with Mikel Arteta’s side straight back into last term’s groove. Arsenal visit Sunderland, a fixture they will be wary of after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last season. The Gunners made it four wins from four with a 1-0 victory at Napoli in their Champions League opener on Wednesday night and – with three victories in the Premier League already under their belt – show no signs of faltering. Billy Munday liveblogs the match and Louise Taylor reports.

Rugby union

10pmSouth Africa v New Zealand live

After three bruising contests, South Africa go in search of a third successive Test victory over ⁠the All Blacks that would secure the four-game series for the world champions and lay down a marker for next year’s title defence. The ⁠final game of New ⁠Zealand’s six-week, ​eight-match tour of South Africa is being played in the United States as the top-ranked sides in the world look ⁠to promote the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series to a wider audience at the 70,000-seater home of the NFL’s Baltimore Ravens. Daniel Gallan buckles up as blog host.

Sunday

Boxing

3amRyan Garcia v Conor Benn live

Ryan Garcia enters his WBC welterweight title fight showdown with Conor Benn carrying the belt but understanding that winning the belt and establishing himself as a legitimate champion are different accomplishments. The American captured the first recognised world title of his turbulent career in February, dominating his compatriot Mario Barrios over 12 rounds for a unanimous decision. The performance showcased a more disciplined, complete fighter than the social media phenomenon who built his reputation on blinding speed and a devastating left hook. Now he must prove that victory began a sustained championship run. His first defence comes at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, where personal hostility and contrasting styles should produce a revealing test. The British fighter intends to pressure Garcia, force exchanges and make the fight physical. Bryan Armen Graham has round-by-round coverage of the big fight.

Football

8amMatchday live

Emillia Hawkins clocks on bright and early to preview Sunday’s action with breaking news and much more as we settle down for two Premier League fixtures, with all the noise around the afternoon’s Manchester derby. Email matchday.live@theguardian.com with your notions and queries.

Golf

10.10amSolheim Cup live

Scott Murray is back at post for the deciding singles contests as Europe seek to regain the trophy after losing 15½-12½ in Virginia two years ago in the biggest team event in women’s golf.

Women’s Super League

12pmManchester United v Chelsea live

Emillia Hawkins then turns to live commentary as last season’s fourth- and third-place teams respectively meet for the first time this season, both seeking a first win of the campaign. United lost to London City last weekend as Eva Olid took charge of the club for the first time in the WSL while Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea were held by Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge despite battering the visitors with 35 shots. Suzanne Wrack reports.

Scottish League Cup quarter-final

12pmRangers v Celtic live

The Hoops’ only blemish this term remains their Champions League playoff capitulation away to Lask, and overcoming their Old Firm rivals at Ibrox to reach the semi-final of the Premier Sports Cup would help maintain their momentum. There will, however, be no Celtic fans in attendance after the recent decision not to allow away supporters at any matches between the two Glasgow giants this term to avoid the trouble that marred last season’s Scottish Cup collision. The anxiety from the Light Blues legions, which has been prevalent in some games in Govan, resurfaced on Wednesday night as the home side struggled in the Premiership match against St Mirren after missing several chances before the break. However, a pressure valve was released when Bojan Miovski scored in stoppage time for a crucial 1-0 win, making it four victories in a row for Derek McInnes and his side. Taha Hashim liveblogs the cup tie, and Paul MacInnes reports.

Formula One

2pmSpanish Grand Prix

John Brewin has lap-by-lap coverage as Formula One sweeps into Madrid for a first look at the Madring. Mercedes are in the ascendant and Kimi Antonelli can still put the equivalent of three race wins between him and Russell, with the Briton chasing a first win since Austria in June to prevent his title hopes from withering further. McLaren, who won in the Netherlands and Hungary with the reigning world champion, Lando Norris, and have Oscar Piastri hungry to open his account, could be the main rivals. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc drove the Madring when it was still a building site on a scorching filming day in July but there is an underlying tension in the camp after last weekend’s opening-lap shenanigans at Monza.

Premier League

4.30pmManchester United v Manchester City live

After all the pre-season optimism, United’s start to the season has been inconsistent but Sunday’s derby offers Michael Carrick’s side an early chance ⁠to show they are contenders. City, meanwhile, arrive at Old Trafford with a perfect record under their new manager, Enzo Maresca, although their performances have suggested there is still work to do after Pep Guardiola’s departure. Carrick’s impact at United last season as interim manager after the club’s parting of ways with Ruben Amorim in January was dramatic, beginning with a 2-0 home victory over City. Their rivals will provide an acid test, especially with Erling Haaland firing on all cylinders having scored both goals in the 2-0 win at Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday to make it five goals in three games so far this season. Rob Smyth liveblogs the big game of the weekend, with Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin reporting from Old Trafford.

Tennis

7pmUS Open men’s singles final

The men’s singles semis pitted Alexander Zverev against Karen Khachanov and Frances Tiafoe with Ben Shelton. The latter pairing are on a quest to become the first American men’s grand slam champion ⁠since Andy Roddick’s 2003 triumph at Flushing Meadows. Whoever emerges victorious will collide in Sunday evening’s final, and Ella Brockway has live blog commentary of the showdown.

items.title: Pochettino’s ‘different’ vow to the US invites unwelcome speculation
items.author: Jeff Rueter
items.summary: I hope, in this lifetime, you find someone who loves you the way Mauricio Pochettino loves Tottenham Hotspur. The grip Spurs have on his heart seems the stuff
items.text:
I hope, in this lifetime, you find someone who loves you the way Mauricio Pochettino loves Tottenham Hotspur. The grip Spurs have on his heart seems the stuff of a literary classic: his imperfect partner who called things off at the first sign of trouble must merely check in on him occasionally to rekindle hopes of a reunion.

Perhaps a bit extreme, but this week’s revelation – that he’d return to Tottenham even if they were relegated and chalking his absence up to imperfect timing, not the part about handing the club a decade-old title – has implicity laid out the terms of his return as United States manager. Others may always have interest in his services, and a certain North London suitor will never get the door slammed in their face outright.

“Now it’s a four-year contract, it’s different,” Pochettino said this week. “We can next season lose the Copa América or the Gold Cup, they’re not happy with us and they can sack us. Or we can say: ‘OK. It’s not in the way that we think.’ Four years is different. Maybe now if someone calls in the future, it’s a different, different type [of thing]. We are excited, we are thinking to spend four years to the next World Cup. But now it’s a long period.”

If you’re a Spurs fan, it warms the heart to revisit last decade’s glory days. If you’re a US fan, you’re quite sick of hearing so much about a team besides the one he’s managing. If you’ve been cursed to support both, this must be a very confusing time. And if you’re US Soccer, you know that you no longer have an ace in the hole to outflank any outside interest.

One can’t undersell the appeal of coaching a World Cup host team, with a direct path to Pot One and raucous support for every match. Already a familiar face to Americans who follow the sport, Pochettino became a genuine sensation in the broader sports landscape. Millions of Americans had parallel thoughts that he, clad handsomely in a $500 safari shirt, resembled Russell Crowe – perhaps tacitly revealing that millions of Americans have long undersold the appeal of Russell Crowe.

Compared to his previous post at Chelsea, the US job offered relative reprieve. Never before has Pochettino been such a prolific fixture on hours-long podcasts. The stop/start cadence of international management is appealing for the football men who have grown weary of the meticulous corporatization of the club game. In that sense, Pochettino is among esteemed company.

Two years after Jürgen Klopp left Liverpool citing mental exhaustion, he has refreshed his tracksuit collection with fresh duds from Die Mannschaft. In his opening press conference, he read aloud to the press his terms of service – and was celebrated for it. Carlo Ancelotti was in no rush to abandon Brazil after a middling tournament, despite real questions about the pool’s depth and quality in midfield. Even Pep Guardiola held talks with Italy immediately after his decade in Manchester.

What’s different about Pochettino from, say, Klopp is his perceived eagerness to return to the club grind. Even atop the Red Bull Football conglomerate, Klopp was quick to brush aside any insinuations about returning to management. Pochettino, by contrast, held talks with Milan about their coaching vacancy immediately before the 2026 World Cup.

Free newsletter | Twice weekly

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

skip past newsletter promotion

There may be a simple answer. Each of Ancelotti, Guardiola, and Klopp – company with which Pochettino is regularly associated – has been the champion of England and Europe. Pochettino, at this stage, has not reached those summits.

Is aiming for a Copa América semi-final more enticing than restoring Tottenham to previous heights? What about reaching a World Cup quarter-final an ocean away from the tens of thousands who soundtracked the previous one? What can US Soccer offer that his caliber of clubs – Tottenham and beyond – can’t exceed?

While Pochettino and his charges have something resembling an excuse for their lack of execution against Belgium, the fact remains that the USMNT were once again eliminated in the last-16. Just like they were under Bob Bradley in 2010. And Jürgen Klinsmann in 2014. And Gregg Berhalter in 2022.

In theory, Pochettino will enter his second cycle in a position of strength having undertaken a thorough examination of the player pool. The fresh faces are no longer MLS journeymen or players in Europe’s lesser divisions. Instead, they’re promising prospects: 16-year-old wonderkid Cavan Sullivan, new Crystal Palace showman Zavier Gozo, highly anticipated La Masia netminder Diego Kochen.

If anything, working the up-and-comers into the established core and identifying sturdier central defenders to partner with Chris Richards should be an incredibly exciting project. The core is in great shape, with this summer’s headliners – Folarin Balogun, Alex Freeman, Richards, and Malik Tillman – all aged 30 or younger in the summer of 2030. There’s plenty of reason to think that the program is better positioned for a deep run at the next World Cup than the 2026.

Actualizing that potential will require a clear vision and a dedicated effort to raise this team’s standard throughout every window of the next four years. Batting eyelashes at past employers hardly projects that level of dedication. And so, for the next four years just like the past one, the biggest question surrounding the USMNT won’t be how far they can go in 2030. It’ll be whether Pochettino will still be the man leading them there.

Millions of Americans had parallel thoughts that he, clad handsomely in a $500 safari shirt, resembled Russell Crowe – perhaps tacitly revealing that millions of Americans have long undersold the appeal of Russell Crowe.

Compared to his previous post at Chelsea, the US job offered relative reprieve. Never before has Pochettino been such a prolific fixture on hours-long podcasts. The stop/start cadence of international management is appealing for the football men who have grown weary of the meticulous corporatization of the club game. In that sense, Pochettino is among esteemed company.

Two years after Jürgen Klopp left Liverpool citing mental exhaustion, he has refreshed his tracksuit collection with fresh duds from Die Mannschaft. In his opening press conference, he read aloud to the press his terms of service – and was celebrated for it. Carlo Ancelotti was in no rush to abandon Brazil after a middling tournament, despite real questions about the pool’s depth and quality in midfield. Even Pep Guardiola held talks with Italy immediately after his decade in Manchester.

What’s different about Pochettino from, say, Klopp is his perceived eagerness to return to the club grind. Even atop the Red Bull Football conglomerate, Klopp was quick to brush aside any insinuations about returning to management. Pochettino, by contrast, held talks with Milan about their coaching vacancy immediately before the 2026 World Cup.

There may be a simple answer. Each of Ancelotti, Guardiola, and Klopp – company with which Pochettino is regularly associated – has been the champion of England and Europe. Pochettino, at this stage, has not reached those summits.

Is aiming for a Copa América semi-final more enticing than restoring Tottenham to previous heights? What about reaching a World Cup quarter-final an ocean away from the tens of thousands who soundtracked the previous one? What can US Soccer offer that his caliber of clubs – Tottenham and beyond – can’t exceed?

While Pochettino and his charges have something resembling an excuse for their lack of execution against Belgium, the fact remains that the USMNT were once again eliminated in the last-16. Just like they were under Bob Bradley in 2010. And Jürgen Klinsmann in 2014. And Gregg Berhalter in 2022.

In theory, Pochettino will enter his second cycle in a position of strength having undertaken a thorough examination of the player pool. The fresh faces are no longer MLS journeymen or players in Europe’s lesser divisions. Instead, they’re promising prospects: 16-year-old wonderkid Cavan Sullivan, new Crystal Palace showman Zavier Gozo, highly anticipated La Masia netminder Diego Kochen.

If anything, working the up-and-comers into the established core and identifying sturdier central defenders to partner with Chris Richards should be an incredibly exciting project. The core is in great shape, with this summer’s headliners – Folarin Balogun, Alex Freeman, Richards, and Malik Tillman – all aged 30 or younger in the summer of 2030. There’s plenty of reason to think that the program is better positioned for a deep run at the next World Cup than the 2026.

Actualizing that potential will require a clear vision and a dedicated effort to raise this team’s standard throughout every window of the next four years. Batting eyelashes at past employers hardly projects that level of dedication. And so, for the next four years just like the past one, the biggest question surrounding the USMNT won’t be how far they can go in 2030. It’ll be whether Pochettino will still be the man leading them there.
