The table clearly shows the trade-off. Hepburn gives you "shi," "chi," "tsu," "fu," and "ji"; these are forms an English reader can pronounce correctly on the first try. Kunrei-shiki gives you "si," "ti," "tu," "hu," and "zi"; these are forms that are regular and predictable from the kana, but that an English reader will mispronounce.

Why was Kunrei-shiki the official system for so long? It was because it is more systematic, reflects Japanese phonology more accurately, and is easier for Japanese people to learn as a set of rules. It maps the kana table onto the alphabet in a consistent grid. Why did Hepburn win in practice? It was because it is what the rest of the world uses. Textbooks published outside Japan use Hepburn. Passports use Hepburn. Road signs use Hepburn. Train stations use Hepburn. The internet uses Hepburn. The official system and the practical system disagreed for seventy years, and in December 2025, the Japanese government resolved the disagreement by making Hepburn official.

What practitioners say #

The trade-off between the two systems is not abstract. Linguists and teachers who have worked in Japan describe the consequences directly.

Neil Kubler, a linguist who has written textbooks on both Chinese and Japanese, points out that Kunrei-shiki has a real pedagogical advantage: "Kunreisiki is better for representing the Japanese sound system from the point of view of native speakers. Kunreisiki is also better for serious Japanese learners as it greatly simplifies the description of Japanese grammar: cf. matu/matte/matimasu (all with the same verb stem mat-) vs. Hepburn matsu/matte/machimasu (with 3 different verb stems)."

Joseph Tomei, who has taught in Japan for over thirty years, describes the real-world fallout: "The fight between Hepburn and Kunrei was so bitter and inconclusive that the government, to try and split the baby, had Hepburn for 'outward facing' uses (i.e. when foreigners might use/read it) while Kunrei was for 'inward use'. So transport signage was in Hepburn, but some government documents and other uses was in Kunrei. This was a particular problem when Japanese started getting credit cards, because Shoji Chiba on a passport would be Syozi Tiba and be rejected."

The 2025 standardization is, in part, a response to exactly this kind of confusion.

Why Japan Made Hepburn Official in 2025 #

On December 22, 2025, the Japanese government issued a cabinet notification establishing Hepburn romanization as the national standard. It was the first revision of the national romanization rules in approximately seventy years.

The reasoning was straightforward: Hepburn was already the de facto standard in passports, road signs, train stations, and international communication. The official system, Kunrei-shiki, and the practical system, Hepburn, had diverged, creating inconsistency between what the rules said and what everyone actually did. Government documents used one system; the signs on the street used another. Making Hepburn official aligned the rules with reality.

What this means for learners is simpler than what came before: the system your textbook uses, the system your dictionary uses, and the system on Japanese street signs are now the same system. You no longer need to translate between official and practical romanization. One system, one set of rules, everywhere.

How Fink uses Hepburn #

Fink puts a pronunciation line in the Insights panel under every Japanese translation, and the system it uses is Hepburn romanization with macrons for long vowels. If you translate a sentence into Japanese and open the Insights panel, the pronunciation line shows you how to say it, written in letters you already know.

Why Hepburn and not IPA? Because a learner who cannot yet read kana does not need a third unfamiliar system between themselves and the text. The International Phonetic Alphabet is a powerful tool, but it requires learning a new set of symbols before you can read a single word. Hepburn uses the letters you already know and gives you sounds to work with immediately. You can read Tōkyō and get close to the right pronunciation without learning anything first. That is the whole point of the system, and it is the reason Fink chose it. For more on when IPA is the right tool and when romanization is better, see Understanding IPA.

The exact scheme is named explicitly in the prompt: "Hepburn romanization, with macrons for long vowels." Never "the pronunciation." A model asked vaguely will invent a different convention every time, and a pronunciation system that changes between requests is worse than none, because you cannot build a habit on it. Naming the system is what makes the pronunciation line consistent, and consistency is what makes it useful.

How to use romanization when learning Japanese #

Romanization is a scaffold, not a destination. Here is how to use it well:

Read the romanization before checking the definition. When you look up a word, sound it out from the Hepburn transcription first, then check the meaning. This builds the connection between sound and word.

Say it aloud. Pronunciation is a physical habit. Reading a sound silently does not build it; saying it does.

Use romanization as a bridge to kana, not as a replacement. The goal is to outgrow it. Once you can read hiragana and katakana, the romanization becomes a check rather than a crutch, and most learners stop needing it after a few months.

Notice the recurring patterns. After a while, you start to see that し is always "shi," that long vowels always get macrons, that the particle は is always "wa." The rules become automatic, and the romanization fades into the background.

This is the same loop described in How to use a translator to learn a language: look up a word, read the pronunciation, say it, notice the pattern. Romanization is what makes that loop work for Japanese, because it is the step that connects the written form to the sound without requiring you to know the writing system yet.

The short answer #

Hepburn romanization is the most widely used system for writing Japanese in the Latin alphabet, popularized in 1867 by an American missionary so that English speakers could pronounce Japanese words correctly, though developed by the Rōmaji-kai, a society of Japanese and foreign scholars. It prioritizes pronunciation over systematic kana-to-romaji mapping, which is why it writes し as "shi" and ち as "chi" even though those break the regular pattern. Japan made it the national standard in December 2025, aligning official rules with what the world was already doing. Fink includes Hepburn romanization in its insights for every Japanese translation, because someone learning Japanese needs sounds they can read, not a third writing system to learn first.

Questions people ask about Hepburn romanization #

Is Hepburn romanization the same as romaji? Romaji means "Roman letters" and refers to any romanization system for Japanese. Hepburn is one specific system, the most widely used one. Kunrei-shiki and Nihon-shiki are also romaji. So "romaji" is the category, and "Hepburn" is one member of it.

Why does Hepburn use "shi" instead of "si"? Because "shi" is closer to how し sounds to an English speaker. "Si" would be pronounced like the English word "see," which is wrong. Hepburn prioritizes pronunciation over systematic kana mapping, and this is the defining example of that choice.

What's the difference between Hepburn and Kunrei-shiki? Hepburn is phonetic for English speakers: し is "shi," ち is "chi," つ is "tsu," ふ is "fu." Kunrei-shiki is systematic: し is "si," ち is "ti," つ is "tu," ふ is "hu." Kunrei-shiki was the official system in Japan from 1954 until December 2025, when Hepburn replaced it as the national standard.

Do I need to learn romanization to learn Japanese? No, but it helps in the early stages. Use it as a bridge to kana, not a replacement for it. Most learners stop needing romanization after a few months, once they can read hiragana and katakana reliably.

Why does Fink use Hepburn instead of IPA for Japanese? Because someone who cannot yet read kana does not need a third unfamiliar system. Hepburn uses letters they already know and gives them sounds to work with immediately. IPA would add a layer of symbols to learn before the actual language. For languages written in the Latin alphabet, Fink does use IPA, the choice depends on the script.

What is Modified Hepburn? Modified Hepburn, also called Revised Hepburn, is the modern standard version of the system. It regularized a few edge cases from the original 1867 dictionary: most notably, it uses "n" before consonants instead of "m" (so しんぶん is "shinbun," not "shimbun"), and it uses macrons for all long vowels consistently. Traditional Hepburn used "m" before b, m, and p, so 新聞 was "shimbun." Modified Hepburn fixes this to "shinbun." When people say "Hepburn" today, they almost always mean Modified Hepburn.

Where is Hepburn romanization used? Road signs, train station names, passports, textbooks published outside Japan, most dictionaries, and the internet at large. Since December 2025, it is also the official national romanization standard of Japan. If you have seen Japanese written in Latin letters, you have almost certainly seen Hepburn.

ち is "chi," not "ti"
つ is "tsu," not "tu"
ふ is "fu," not "hu"
じ is "ji," not "zi"

These are the forms that make Hepburn pronounceable to an English reader. "Shi" sounds like し. "Si" would sound like the English word "see," which is wrong. The trade-off is that these forms break the one-to-one correspondence between kana and romanization, which is exactly what competing systems like Kunrei-shiki fix.
https://www.fink-translate.com/assets/blog/hepburn-romanization/kana-chart.png

blocks.x: Long vowels and macrons #
Japanese distinguishes between short and long vowels, and the distinction changes meaning. In Hepburn, long vowels are marked with a macron: a line over the letter. ō, ū, ā, ē, ī.
Tōkyō (東京), the long "o" in both syllables
Ōsaka (大阪), the long "o" at the start
kyū (九, "nine"), the long "u"
obāsan (おばあさん, "grandmother") vs obasan (おばさん, "aunt"), the macron is the only difference, and it changes who you are talking about

Macrons matter because they carry information. The common simplification is to drop them in casual contexts: Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto. This is acceptable for proper nouns that are already known to the reader, but it strips pronunciation information for learners. A learner reading "Tokyo" and sounding it out in English will say something closer to "toe-key-oh," which is not how any Japanese speaker says it.
Passports and long vowels #

Japanese passports do not use macrons. A long "o" is written as "oh," "oo," or "ou" depending on the kanji, and a long "u" becomes "uu." Someone named 大野 gets "Ohno" on their passport, and 久保 becomes "Kubo" without the long vowel marked at all. This is a practical compromise: macrons are not available on every form and do not appear in every database, so the passport system uses letter combinations that any system can handle. It is not Hepburn in the strict sense, but it is the closest approximation the passport format allows. The result is that the same person's name can look different on their passport, in a textbook, and on a road sign, which is one of the frictions the 2025 standardization is meant to reduce.
The syllabic n and the apostrophe #

The syllable ん, written as "n" in Hepburn, is a nasal sound that can appear at the end of a word or before a consonant. Most of the time it is straightforward: san (さん), shinbun (新聞, "newspaper"), nihon (日本, "Japan").

The apostrophe enters when ん comes before a vowel or a "y" sound. Without it, the romanization is ambiguous. kin'en (禁煙, "no smoking") and kinen (記念, "commemoration") are different words. The apostrophe separates the "n" from the following vowel so you know it is a consonant, not part of a syllable like "ne." The same rule applies to names: Jun'ichirō vs Junichirō, where the apostrophe tells you the "n" is not part of a "ni" syllable.

This is the rule that most casual romanization ignores. It is also the one that causes the most ambiguity, because without the apostrophe, two different Japanese words can romanize to the same string.
The particles は, を, へ #
Japanese has three grammatical particles that are pronounced differently from how their kana would suggest. Hepburn writes what you hear:
は is "wa" when used as a particle, not "ha" (its reading as a regular syllable)
を is "o" when used as a particle, not "wo"
へ is "e" when used as a particle, not "he"

This reflects a historical shift. The kana spelling preserves an older pronunciation that no longer exists, but Hepburn follows modern pronunciation. A sentence like わたしは is written "watashi wa," because that is what it sounds like.
Doubled consonants #
The small っ, called sokuon, indicates a geminate consonant: a consonant held twice as long. In Hepburn, this is written by doubling the following consonant.
kitte (切手, "stamp"), the "tt" is held
matte (待って, "wait"), the "tt" is held
kippu (切符, "ticket"), the "pp" is held
The doubled consonant is a real phonetic feature, not just a spelling convention. If you do not hold the consonant, you get a different word: kite (着て, "wear") vs kitte (切手, "stamp").
Hepburn writes what you hear, not what the kana spells. That is why a particle pronounced "wa" is written "wa" even when its kana is は.
Hepburn vs. Kunrei-shiki vs. Nihon-shiki #

Hepburn is not the only romanization system for Japanese. Two others matter: Nihon-shiki, designed in 1885, and Kunrei-shiki, a simplified version of Nihon-shiki that became the official Japanese standard in 1937 and was reaffirmed in 1954.

The difference comes down to a single design decision and its consequences. Hepburn optimizes for pronunciation by English speakers. Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki optimize for a systematic, one-to-one mapping between kana and romanization. One kana, one romanization, always, with no exceptions.

ぢ

The table clearly shows the trade-off. Hepburn gives you "shi," "chi," "tsu," "fu," and "ji"; these are forms an English reader can pronounce correctly on the first try. Kunrei-shiki gives you "si," "ti," "tu," "hu," and "zi"; these are forms that are regular and predictable from the kana, but that an English reader will mispronounce.

Why was Kunrei-shiki the official system for so long? It was because it is more systematic, reflects Japanese phonology more accurately, and is easier for Japanese people to learn as a set of rules. It maps the kana table onto the alphabet in a consistent grid. Why did Hepburn win in practice? It was because it is what the rest of the world uses. Textbooks published outside Japan use Hepburn. Passports use Hepburn. Road signs use Hepburn. Train stations use Hepburn. The internet uses Hepburn. The official system and the practical system disagreed for seventy years, and in December 2025, the Japanese government resolved the disagreement by making Hepburn official.
What practitioners say #
The trade-off between the two systems is not abstract. Linguists and teachers who have worked in Japan describe the consequences directly.

Neil Kubler, a linguist who has written textbooks on both Chinese and Japanese, points out that Kunrei-shiki has a real pedagogical advantage: "Kunreisiki is better for representing the Japanese sound system from the point of view of native speakers. Kunreisiki is also better for serious Japanese learners as it greatly simplifies the description of Japanese grammar: cf. matu/matte/matimasu (all with the same verb stem mat-) vs. Hepburn matsu/matte/machimasu (with 3 different verb stems)."

Joseph Tomei, who has taught in Japan for over thirty years, describes the real-world fallout: "The fight between Hepburn and Kunrei was so bitter and inconclusive that the government, to try and split the baby, had Hepburn for 'outward facing' uses (i.e. when foreigners might use/read it) while Kunrei was for 'inward use'. So transport signage was in Hepburn, but some government documents and other uses was in Kunrei. This was a particular problem when Japanese started getting credit cards, because Shoji Chiba on a passport would be Syozi Tiba and be rejected."
The 2025 standardization is, in part, a response to exactly this kind of confusion.
Why Japan Made Hepburn Official in 2025 #

On December 22, 2025, the Japanese government issued a cabinet notification establishing Hepburn romanization as the national standard. It was the first revision of the national romanization rules in approximately seventy years.

The reasoning was straightforward: Hepburn was already the de facto standard in passports, road signs, train stations, and international communication. The official system, Kunrei-shiki, and the practical system, Hepburn, had diverged, creating inconsistency between what the rules said and what everyone actually did. Government documents used one system; the signs on the street used another. Making Hepburn official aligned the rules with reality.

What this means for learners is simpler than what came before: the system your textbook uses, the system your dictionary uses, and the system on Japanese street signs are now the same system. You no longer need to translate between official and practical romanization. One system, one set of rules, everywhere.
How Fink uses Hepburn #

Fink puts a pronunciation line in the Insights panel under every Japanese translation, and the system it uses is Hepburn romanization with macrons for long vowels. If you translate a sentence into Japanese and open the Insights panel, the pronunciation line shows you how to say it, written in letters you already know.
https://www.fink-translate.com/assets/blog/hepburn-romanization/insights-panel.png
blocks.c: The Insights panel with meaning notes, a Hepburn pronunciation line for a Japanese translation, and a back translation, each labelled.

blocks.x: https://www.fink-translate.com/assets/blog/hepburn-romanization/insights-panel-dark.png
blocks.c: The Insights panel with meaning notes, a Hepburn pronunciation line for a Japanese translation, and a back translation, each labelled.

blocks.x: Why Hepburn and not IPA? Because a learner who cannot yet read kana does not need a third unfamiliar system between themselves and the text. The International Phonetic Alphabet is a powerful tool, but it requires learning a new set of symbols before you can read a single word. Hepburn uses the letters you already know and gives you sounds to work with immediately. You can read Tōkyō and get close to the right pronunciation without learning anything first. That is the whole point of the system, and it is the reason Fink chose it. For more on when IPA is the right tool and when romanization is better, see Understanding IPA.

The exact scheme is named explicitly in the prompt: "Hepburn romanization, with macrons for long vowels." Never "the pronunciation." A model asked vaguely will invent a different convention every time, and a pronunciation system that changes between requests is worse than none, because you cannot build a habit on it. Naming the system is what makes the pronunciation line consistent, and consistency is what makes it useful.
How to use romanization when learning Japanese #
Romanization is a scaffold, not a destination. Here is how to use it well:

Read the romanization before checking the definition. When you look up a word, sound it out from the Hepburn transcription first, then check the meaning. This builds the connection between sound and word.
Say it aloud. Pronunciation is a physical habit. Reading a sound silently does not build it; saying it does.

Use romanization as a bridge to kana, not as a replacement. The goal is to outgrow it. Once you can read hiragana and katakana, the romanization becomes a check rather than a crutch, and most learners stop needing it after a few months.

Notice the recurring patterns. After a while, you start to see that し is always "shi," that long vowels always get macrons, that the particle は is always "wa." The rules become automatic, and the romanization fades into the background.

This is the same loop described in How to use a translator to learn a language: look up a word, read the pronunciation, say it, notice the pattern. Romanization is what makes that loop work for Japanese, because it is the step that connects the written form to the sound without requiring you to know the writing system yet.
The short answer #

Hepburn romanization is the most widely used system for writing Japanese in the Latin alphabet, popularized in 1867 by an American missionary so that English speakers could pronounce Japanese words correctly, though developed by the Rōmaji-kai, a society of Japanese and foreign scholars. It prioritizes pronunciation over systematic kana-to-romaji mapping, which is why it writes し as "shi" and ち as "chi" even though those break the regular pattern. Japan made it the national standard in December 2025, aligning official rules with what the world was already doing. Fink includes Hepburn romanization in its insights for every Japanese translation, because someone learning Japanese needs sounds they can read, not a third writing system to learn first.
Questions people ask about Hepburn romanization #

Is Hepburn romanization the same as romaji? Romaji means "Roman letters" and refers to any romanization system for Japanese. Hepburn is one specific system, the most widely used one. Kunrei-shiki and Nihon-shiki are also romaji. So "romaji" is the category, and "Hepburn" is one member of it.

Why does Hepburn use "shi" instead of "si"? Because "shi" is closer to how し sounds to an English speaker. "Si" would be pronounced like the English word "see," which is wrong. Hepburn prioritizes pronunciation over systematic kana mapping, and this is the defining example of that choice.

What's the difference between Hepburn and Kunrei-shiki? Hepburn is phonetic for English speakers: し is "shi," ち is "chi," つ is "tsu," ふ is "fu." Kunrei-shiki is systematic: し is "si," ち is "ti," つ is "tu," ふ is "hu." Kunrei-shiki was the official system in Japan from 1954 until December 2025, when Hepburn replaced it as the national standard.

Do I need to learn romanization to learn Japanese? No, but it helps in the early stages. Use it as a bridge to kana, not a replacement for it. Most learners stop needing romanization after a few months, once they can read hiragana and katakana reliably.

Why does Fink use Hepburn instead of IPA for Japanese? Because someone who cannot yet read kana does not need a third unfamiliar system. Hepburn uses letters they already know and gives them sounds to work with immediately. IPA would add a layer of symbols to learn before the actual language. For languages written in the Latin alphabet, Fink does use IPA, the choice depends on the script.

What is Modified Hepburn? Modified Hepburn, also called Revised Hepburn, is the modern standard version of the system. It regularized a few edge cases from the original 1867 dictionary: most notably, it uses "n" before consonants instead of "m" (so しんぶん is "shinbun," not "shimbun"), and it uses macrons for all long vowels consistently. Traditional Hepburn used "m" before b, m, and p, so 新聞 was "shimbun." Modified Hepburn fixes this to "shinbun." When people say "Hepburn" today, they almost always mean Modified Hepburn.

Where is Hepburn romanization used? Road signs, train station names, passports, textbooks published outside Japan, most dictionaries, and the internet at large. Since December 2025, it is also the official national romanization standard of Japan. If you have seen Japanese written in Latin letters, you have almost certainly seen Hepburn.

items.text:
This post covers material from a talk I gave at Latency Conference. If you want to just:

You read that correctly, Pandas should go extinct. Not the cute fluffy things used for international diplomacy, but the Python DataFrame library.

Why? Because Pandas’ inefficiencies force you to adopt distributed querying systems before your workloads justify the added complexity. I posit that most workloads will never justify those systems, they are just well marketed “silver bullets”.

To understand what I’m talking about we first must understand the typical adoption pathway for Pandas.

The diagram below shows a rough guide of when you typically would consider adopting a given DataFrame library based on the data size you are working with. Following it from left to right, you also see the typical adoption pathway for data analysis tools, and the cliff that Pandas’ users experience beyond a certain data size.

People typically start with Excel and graduate to Pandas somewhere in the GB range. Pandas serves them well into the 10s of GBs range, and then they start hitting memory issues, slow computation, or become frustrated with Pandas’ baroque API. The traditional answer at this point is to graduate to a “real” (read: expensive) tool like Spark, DataBricks, Snowflake, or Dask designed for Big Data ™️

Here’s the thing: there’s a growing gap between the “Pandas cliff” and the scale where distributed systems are genuinely necessary. This gap, sits somewhere around the 100GB mark, and can be effectively filled by modern, high-performance, single-machine tools. I’m primarily talking about Polars and DuckDB.

Why do we care so much about this ~100GB threshold? The answer lies in understanding how much “Big Data” exists in the wild.

In 2024, Amazon published a paper entitled “Why TPC is not enough: An analysis of the Amazon Redshift fleet”. The aim of this paper was to compare telemetry data from Amazon’s own distributed analytics database, Redshift, with the query patterns used in industry standard database benchmarks. As part of their analysis Amazon published fleet statistics on query run times and table sizes.

If we’re willing to make a couple of assumptions we draw some interesting conclusions about how Amazon’s customers are using analytics databases. Let’s assume that:

The average size of a row in a Redshift table is 1KB

Every RedShift cluster is comprised of 10 machines that are each capable of guzzling data at 8GB/s from S3, and do nothing but this

We find that:

94.68% of tables in the Redshift fleet contain fewer than 100GB of data

86.9% of queries operate on 80GB of data or less

If you are interested in another, deeper look at this dataset, Jordan Tigani of MotherDuck did a deep dive here. Note: MotherDuck is a SaaS business selling DuckDB hosting, so some scepticism is perhaps warranted.

Summing up the first 3 rows of the runtime table we calculate that 86.9% of queries run in less than a second.

Using our assumptions that we have 10 machines in the cluster guzzling data at 8GB/s we compute:

10 machines * 8GB * 1 second = 80GB of data

The assumption of 8GB/s is based on this admittedly outdated benchmark.

To arrive at the claim of “94.68% of tables contain less than 100GB” we sum the rows up to the 10^8 limit, giving us 94.68% of rows. We then take our assumption of 1KB per row and compute:

10^8 rows in a table * 1KB = 100GB

Perhaps the assumption of 1KB/row is too optimistic, but even assuming 10KB, you still arrive at a table size of 1TB.

You likely do not have Big Data, and probably never will. You have Medium Data problems, and need Medium Data solutions.

The alternatives I propose, as alluded to earlier are DuckDB and Polars. In broad strokes, Polars is a Rust-based DataFrame library that feels familiar to Pandas, but differs in several important ways we will explore. DuckDB is an in-memory analytics DB - essentially SQLite for analytics. To get a feel for these tools and how they differ from Pandas let’s look at an example.

The 1 Billion Row Challenge was a challenge to write the fastest Java program which could compute the min, mean and max of a 1 billion row CSV containing weather station data. The fastest implementation accepted for the competition ran in 1.5 seconds.

The original challenge used a bare metal Hetzner AX161 server with 32 cores and 128GB of RAM running Debian 12. Because the author is a serial procrastinator, a skinflint and Hetzner requires you to develop a “reputation” in order to rent large boxes, a m7a.8xlarge from AWS was instead used for these tests, also running Debian 12.

This fundamental configuration is the same as the original challenge: 32 cores and 128GB of RAM on an AMD CPU. However not using bare metal dedicated hardware may affect reproducibility somewhat(sorry).

Without further ado, let’s look at some implementations.

This should look very familiar to anyone who has touched Pandas before. We read the data in from the CSV, group by the weather station and then compute the aggregate min, mean and max figures.

For performance tests the output serialisation specified in the original challenge is skipped. The implementations all include the ability to serialise the output, which was used to unit test the implementations (e.g. the Pandas code). Given that the output format for the 1 Billion Row challenge is non-standard, it didn’t feel like a relevant test of the various libraries to test serialisation.

def do_1brc_pandas(file_path: str):
df = (
pd.read_csv(file_path, sep=";", names=["station", "measurement"])
.groupby("station")
.agg({"measurement": ["min", "mean", "max"]})
.round(2)
)

The key part of this example to remember is that Pandas executes each step of this computation sequentially and eagerly. It reads in the entire dataset, groups it and then performs aggregation.

The Polars code looks similar to Pandas, but it works very differently at runtime as we will see.

def do_1brc_polars(file_path: str):
df = (
pl.scan_csv(
file_path,
separator=";",
new_columns=["station", "measurement"],
has_header=False,
)
.group_by("station")
.agg(
pl.col("measurement").min().round(2).alias("min"),
pl.col("measurement").mean().round(2).alias("mean"),
pl.col("measurement").max().round(2).alias("max"),
)
.collect(new_streaming=True) # Stream the input data and perform computations in chunks
)

The data is scanned in chunks, grouped and aggregated. The key detail here is that scan_csv is lazily evaluated and the call to .collect executes the query pipeline. If this sounds like database terminology it should. This lazy evaluation allows Polars to construct an optimised query graph, similar to a database, and leverage 40 years worth of database optimisations to read the data in a chunk-wise fashion and parallelise the work across threads as necessary.

Much like a database, we can visualise the optimised and unoptimised query plan by replacing our call to .collect with a call to .explain(streaming=True) and .explain(streaming=True, optimized=False) respectively.

This query plan isn’t hugely exciting, it scans the CSV, does a 2 column projection, and aggregates. For queries involving filtering we’d expect to see predicate push down applied, where rows are filtered before aggregation occurs. This is unlike Pandas, where all rows are loaded into memory and then filtered.

AGGREGATE
[col("measurement").min().round().alias("min"), col("measurement").mean().round().alias("mean"), col("measurement").max().round().alias("max")] BY [col("station")] FROM
STREAMING:
simple π 2/2 ["measurement", "station"]
Csv SCAN [/Users/eddie/Documents/code/pandas-should-go-extinct/data/measurements.csv]
PROJECT 2/2 COLUMNS

The DuckDB code reads like vanilla SQL - columns are selected with an aggregation function applied and a group by criteria.

def do_1brc_duckdb(file_path: str):
df = duckdb.read_csv(file_path, names=["station", "measurements"])
src = duckdb.sql("""
create table src as
select
station,
min(measurements) min,
max(measurements) max,
cast(avg(measurements) as decimal(8, 1)) avg
from df
group by station
"""
)

The key takeaways from this code sample is that DuckDB provides an SQL interface over your data, however and wherever it is stored. It also has the ability to query Python objects in memory, in the listing above the object df is created by reading the CSV and is queried using SQL.

DuckDB, much like Polars, constructs and executes query plans which are applied in a lazy, multi-threaded, chunk-wise manner depending on if the query engine deems it appropriate. By tacking on a call to .explain() we can also view the query plan that DuckDB generates for the query.

Again, the query plan isn’t hugely exciting, it scans the CSV, does a 2 column projection, and aggregates.

Note: this is the output from running the plan on my M1 MBA, which was not used for performance profiling results below.

Performance was measured by writing a stand-alone script for each library and pointing it at a 1 billion row CSV on disk.

The script was executed from a lightweight hand-rolled benchmark tool which spawns a fresh Python interpreter to run the script and polls memory and CPU metrics on a 50ms interval using psutil until the child process exits. Two warmup iterations were run for each benchmark followed by thirty repetitions of the script.

This approach is by no means perfect, but struck a suitable balance between accuracy and overhead for the purposes of comparison.

The results here truly speak for themselves: Polars and DuckDB are significantly faster than Pandas, using 2x and 19x less memory respectively. They are within striking distance of a hand-tooled Java implementation.

The memory usage of the Polars implementation still seems a little high, I suspect not all the computations were streamed. DuckDB was flawless, giving phenomenal performance with very little code and no tuning.

However, better production performance is only part of the equation. DuckDB and Polars also shine in speeding up your local dev loop.

Let’s repeat the performance tests on powerful, slightly dated laptop hardware. For this test I used a Framework 13 with an Intel i5-1135G7 with 8 cores and 16GB of RAM.

Once again we see great performance from Polars and DuckDB, albeit with Polars consuming significant memory and slightly dipping into swap. Pandas by comparison, runs like molasses and guzzles memory.

This benchmark highlights several key advantages over traditional Pandas workflows:

Painless Multi-threading: Polars and DuckDB automatically use all your CPU cores without you needing to manage threads or processes. You paid for those cores; use them!

Efficient Memory Use & Streaming: Both DuckDB and Polars can process data chunk-wise, which helps reduce memory usage.

Lazy Evaluation: By defining the whole computation upfront, both libraries can optimize the execution plan, applying techniques like predicate pushdown (filtering data early) - just like “real” databases.

Potential Spill-to-Disk: When optimized operations exceed RAM, these tools have built-in mechanisms to intelligently spill intermediate results to disk, which is usually more efficient than relying on the OS’s generic swapping.

If you’re interested in the more standard TPC-H benchmark results, you can find them here.

Note on the TPC-H benchmark results
These TPC-H benchmarks were run by Coiled, a company which provides hosted Dask services, which “competes” with Polars / DuckDB for mind share in this space. That doesn’t mean their benchmarks are wrong, but it’s worth maintaining some scepticism (including of me!).

We’ve all been burned by shiny tools before, some of us are even being burnt by them as we speak. The key to testing out these tools without rewriting everything is Apache Arrow. Arrow is becoming the de facto in-memory representation of columnar data, and is the brain child of the original creator of Pandas, Wes McKinney. Pandas has supported Arrow since its 2.0 release in April 2023.

Polars and DuckDB both support Arrow natively. This means that you can move DataFrames between Polars, Pandas and DuckDB without copying memory, making switching between the frameworks nearly “free”. The one gotcha here is that Pandas doesn’t create Arrow-backed DataFrames by default, you have to specify when you create the DataFrame that you want the dtype_backend to be pyarrow.

Let’s analyze the NYC Taxi dataset (trips from 2009-present, stored in monthly Parquet files) to see if cash payments became less common during the pandemic (2019-2022). This involves processing about 3GB of Parquet data.

For this example we’ll implement functions for reading the parquet files and performing the computation in both DuckDB and Pandas. The Polars version of these functions is left as an exercise to the reader 😉.

The Pandas code:

COLUMNS = ["tpep_pickup_datetime", "payment_type"]
MIN_DATETIME = "2019-01-01"
MAX_DATETIME = "2023-01-01"
# Enum value for cash as the payment type
CASH = 2
def read_data_pandas(folder: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
df = None
for entry in folder.iterdir():
if not entry.name.endswith("parquet"):
continue
temp_df = pd.read_parquet(entry, columns=COLUMNS, dtype_backend="pyarrow")
if df is not None:
df = pd.concat([df, temp_df])
else:
df = temp_df
# Clamp the data to the range we're interested in
df = df[df["tpep_pickup_datetime"] > pd.to_datetime(MIN_DATETIME)]
df = df[df["tpep_pickup_datetime"] < pd.to_datetime(MAX_DATETIME)]
df["month"] = df["tpep_pickup_datetime"].dt.month
df["year"] = df["tpep_pickup_datetime"].dt.year
df = df.drop(["tpep_pickup_datetime"], axis="columns")
return df
def calculate_cash_pandas(df: pd.DataFrame):
df = (
df.groupby(["year", "month", "payment_type"])
.agg({"payment_type": "count"})
.unstack(fill_value=0, level=2)["payment_type"]
.reset_index()
)
df["total_payments"] = df.iloc[:, 2:8].sum(axis=1)
df["cash_pct"] = (df[CASH] / df["total_payments"]) * 100

The DuckDB code:

def read_data_duck(folder: str):
return duckdb.sql(f"""
select
datepart('year', tpep_pickup_datetime) year,
datepart('month', tpep_pickup_datetime) month,
payment_type
from '{folder}/*.parquet'
where
tpep_pickup_datetime > '{MIN_DATE}'
and tpep_pickup_datetime < '{MAX_DATE}'"""
)
def calculate_cash_duck(data):
return duckdb.sql(f"""
with total as (
select year, month, count(payment_type) payments from df
group by year, month
),
total_cash as (
select year, month, count(payment_type) cash from df
where payment_type={CASH}
group by year, month
)
select total.*, cash, (cash / total) * 100 cash_pct from total
join total_cash
on total.year=total_cash.year and total.month=total_cash.month
order by total.year, total.month
""").df() # Force evaluation by materialising to a df otherwise the execution is lazy

We can then matrix these calls to read data and run the calculations together to understand the bang for buck you can get from picking either tool for reading, writing or both.

def pure_pandas(folder: Path):
data = read_data_pandas(folder)
df = calculate_cash_pandas(data)
def duck_reads_panda_thinks(folder: Path):
data = read_data_duck(folder).df()
df = calculate_cash_pandas(data)
def panda_reads_duck_thinks(folder: Path):
data = read_data_pandas(folder)
df = calculate_cash_duck(data)
def pure_duck(folder: Path):
data = read_data_duck(folder)
df = do_taxi_duck_compute(data)

blocks.x: This post covers material from a talk I gave at Latency Conference. If you want to just:
You read that correctly, Pandas should go extinct. Not the cute fluffy things used for international diplomacy, but the Python DataFrame library.

Why? Because Pandas’ inefficiencies force you to adopt distributed querying systems before your workloads justify the added complexity. I posit that most workloads will never justify those systems, they are just well marketed “silver bullets”.
To understand what I’m talking about we first must understand the typical adoption pathway for Pandas.

The diagram below shows a rough guide of when you typically would consider adopting a given DataFrame library based on the data size you are working with. Following it from left to right, you also see the typical adoption pathway for data analysis tools, and the cliff that Pandas’ users experience beyond a certain data size.

People typically start with Excel and graduate to Pandas somewhere in the GB range. Pandas serves them well into the 10s of GBs range, and then they start hitting memory issues, slow computation, or become frustrated with Pandas’ baroque API. The traditional answer at this point is to graduate to a “real” (read: expensive) tool like Spark, DataBricks, Snowflake, or Dask designed for Big Data ™️
https://eddie.codes/_astro/tools_comparison_gap.BGZ5Vh3N_Z1voFSC.webp
blocks.c: A comparison of common DataFrame libraries and the rough data size you'd consider adopting them

blocks.x: Here’s the thing: there’s a growing gap between the “Pandas cliff” and the scale where distributed systems are genuinely necessary. This gap, sits somewhere around the 100GB mark, and can be effectively filled by modern, high-performance, single-machine tools. I’m primarily talking about Polars and DuckDB.
Why do we care so much about this ~100GB threshold? The answer lies in understanding how much “Big Data” exists in the wild.

In 2024, Amazon published a paper entitled “Why TPC is not enough: An analysis of the Amazon Redshift fleet”. The aim of this paper was to compare telemetry data from Amazon’s own distributed analytics database, Redshift, with the query patterns used in industry standard database benchmarks. As part of their analysis Amazon published fleet statistics on query run times and table sizes.
https://eddie.codes/_astro/query_runtime.Ddcpio5U_Zf1Wb7.webp
blocks.c: Bucketed query runtimes for the Amazon Redshift fleet

blocks.x: https://eddie.codes/_astro/table_size.CUNETt92_134m1v.webp
blocks.c: Bucketed table sizes for the Amazon Redshift fleet

blocks.x: If we’re willing to make a couple of assumptions we draw some interesting conclusions about how Amazon’s customers are using analytics databases. Let’s assume that:
The average size of a row in a Redshift table is 1KB
Every RedShift cluster is comprised of 10 machines that are each capable of guzzling data at 8GB/s from S3, and do nothing but this
We find that:
94.68% of tables in the Redshift fleet contain fewer than 100GB of data
86.9% of queries operate on 80GB of data or less

If you are interested in another, deeper look at this dataset, Jordan Tigani of MotherDuck did a deep dive here. Note: MotherDuck is a SaaS business selling DuckDB hosting, so some scepticism is perhaps warranted.
Summing up the first 3 rows of the runtime table we calculate that 86.9% of queries run in less than a second.
Using our assumptions that we have 10 machines in the cluster guzzling data at 8GB/s we compute:
10 machines * 8GB * 1 second = 80GB of data
The assumption of 8GB/s is based on this admittedly outdated benchmark.
To arrive at the claim of “94.68% of tables contain less than 100GB” we sum the rows up to the 10^8 limit, giving us 94.68% of rows. We then take our assumption of 1KB per row and compute:
10^8 rows in a table * 1KB = 100GB
Perhaps the assumption of 1KB/row is too optimistic, but even assuming 10KB, you still arrive at a table size of 1TB.
You likely do not have Big Data, and probably never will. You have Medium Data problems, and need Medium Data solutions.

The alternatives I propose, as alluded to earlier are DuckDB and Polars. In broad strokes, Polars is a Rust-based DataFrame library that feels familiar to Pandas, but differs in several important ways we will explore. DuckDB is an in-memory analytics DB - essentially SQLite for analytics. To get a feel for these tools and how they differ from Pandas let’s look at an example.

The 1 Billion Row Challenge was a challenge to write the fastest Java program which could compute the min, mean and max of a 1 billion row CSV containing weather station data. The fastest implementation accepted for the competition ran in 1.5 seconds.

The original challenge used a bare metal Hetzner AX161 server with 32 cores and 128GB of RAM running Debian 12. Because the author is a serial procrastinator, a skinflint and Hetzner requires you to develop a “reputation” in order to rent large boxes, a m7a.8xlarge from AWS was instead used for these tests, also running Debian 12.

This fundamental configuration is the same as the original challenge: 32 cores and 128GB of RAM on an AMD CPU. However not using bare metal dedicated hardware may affect reproducibility somewhat(sorry).
Without further ado, let’s look at some implementations.
This should look very familiar to anyone who has touched Pandas before. We read the data in from the CSV, group by the weather station and then compute the aggregate min, mean and max figures.

For performance tests the output serialisation specified in the original challenge is skipped. The implementations all include the ability to serialise the output, which was used to unit test the implementations (e.g. the Pandas code). Given that the output format for the 1 Billion Row challenge is non-standard, it didn’t feel like a relevant test of the various libraries to test serialisation.

def do_1brc_pandas(file_path: str):
df = (
pd.read_csv(file_path, sep=";", names=["station", "measurement"])
.groupby("station")
.agg({"measurement": ["min", "mean", "max"]})
.round(2)
)
The key part of this example to remember is that Pandas executes each step of this computation sequentially and eagerly. It reads in the entire dataset, groups it and then performs aggregation.
The Polars code looks similar to Pandas, but it works very differently at runtime as we will see.

def do_1brc_polars(file_path: str):
df = (
pl.scan_csv(
file_path,
separator=";",
new_columns=["station", "measurement"],
has_header=False,
)
.group_by("station")
.agg(
pl.col("measurement").min().round(2).alias("min"),
pl.col("measurement").mean().round(2).alias("mean"),
pl.col("measurement").max().round(2).alias("max"),
)
.collect(new_streaming=True) # Stream the input data and perform computations in chunks
)

The data is scanned in chunks, grouped and aggregated. The key detail here is that scan_csv is lazily evaluated and the call to .collect executes the query pipeline. If this sounds like database terminology it should. This lazy evaluation allows Polars to construct an optimised query graph, similar to a database, and leverage 40 years worth of database optimisations to read the data in a chunk-wise fashion and parallelise the work across threads as necessary.

Much like a database, we can visualise the optimised and unoptimised query plan by replacing our call to .collect with a call to .explain(streaming=True) and .explain(streaming=True, optimized=False) respectively.

This query plan isn’t hugely exciting, it scans the CSV, does a 2 column projection, and aggregates. For queries involving filtering we’d expect to see predicate push down applied, where rows are filtered before aggregation occurs. This is unlike Pandas, where all rows are loaded into memory and then filtered.

AGGREGATE
[col("measurement").min().round().alias("min"), col("measurement").mean().round().alias("mean"), col("measurement").max().round().alias("max")] BY [col("station")] FROM
STREAMING:
simple π 2/2 ["measurement", "station"]
Csv SCAN [/Users/eddie/Documents/code/pandas-should-go-extinct/data/measurements.csv]
PROJECT 2/2 COLUMNS
The DuckDB code reads like vanilla SQL - columns are selected with an aggregation function applied and a group by criteria.

def do_1brc_duckdb(file_path: str):
df = duckdb.read_csv(file_path, names=["station", "measurements"])
src = duckdb.sql("""
create table src as
select
station,
min(measurements) min,
max(measurements) max,
cast(avg(measurements) as decimal(8, 1)) avg
from df
group by station
"""
)

The key takeaways from this code sample is that DuckDB provides an SQL interface over your data, however and wherever it is stored. It also has the ability to query Python objects in memory, in the listing above the object df is created by reading the CSV and is queried using SQL.

DuckDB, much like Polars, constructs and executes query plans which are applied in a lazy, multi-threaded, chunk-wise manner depending on if the query engine deems it appropriate. By tacking on a call to .explain() we can also view the query plan that DuckDB generates for the query.
Again, the query plan isn’t hugely exciting, it scans the CSV, does a 2 column projection, and aggregates.
Note: this is the output from running the plan on my M1 MBA, which was not used for performance profiling results below.
Performance was measured by writing a stand-alone script for each library and pointing it at a 1 billion row CSV on disk.

The script was executed from a lightweight hand-rolled benchmark tool which spawns a fresh Python interpreter to run the script and polls memory and CPU metrics on a 50ms interval using psutil until the child process exits. Two warmup iterations were run for each benchmark followed by thirty repetitions of the script.
This approach is by no means perfect, but struck a suitable balance between accuracy and overhead for the purposes of comparison.

The results here truly speak for themselves: Polars and DuckDB are significantly faster than Pandas, using 2x and 19x less memory respectively. They are within striking distance of a hand-tooled Java implementation.

The memory usage of the Polars implementation still seems a little high, I suspect not all the computations were streamed. DuckDB was flawless, giving phenomenal performance with very little code and no tuning.
However, better production performance is only part of the equation. DuckDB and Polars also shine in speeding up your local dev loop.
Let’s repeat the performance tests on powerful, slightly dated laptop hardware. For this test I used a Framework 13 with an Intel i5-1135G7 with 8 cores and 16GB of RAM.

Once again we see great performance from Polars and DuckDB, albeit with Polars consuming significant memory and slightly dipping into swap. Pandas by comparison, runs like molasses and guzzles memory.
This benchmark highlights several key advantages over traditional Pandas workflows:
Painless Multi-threading: Polars and DuckDB automatically use all your CPU cores without you needing to manage threads or processes. You paid for those cores; use them!
Efficient Memory Use & Streaming: Both DuckDB and Polars can process data chunk-wise, which helps reduce memory usage.

Lazy Evaluation: By defining the whole computation upfront, both libraries can optimize the execution plan, applying techniques like predicate pushdown (filtering data early) - just like “real” databases.

Potential Spill-to-Disk: When optimized operations exceed RAM, these tools have built-in mechanisms to intelligently spill intermediate results to disk, which is usually more efficient than relying on the OS’s generic swapping.
If you’re interested in the more standard TPC-H benchmark results, you can find them here.

Note on the TPC-H benchmark results
These TPC-H benchmarks were run by Coiled, a company which provides hosted Dask services, which “competes” with Polars / DuckDB for mind share in this space. That doesn’t mean their benchmarks are wrong, but it’s worth maintaining some scepticism (including of me!).

items.text:
litellm's routing + translation in ~2,900 lines and 2 dependencies (openai, httpx).

litellm routes LLM calls across providers and translates between message formats. That core is buried under 100k+ LOC of proxy servers, caching layers, cost tracking, and dozens of features most users never touch. litelm extracts just the call path — model routing, message translation, streaming, tool use, embeddings — and nothing else. No Router class, no proxy, no caching.

pip install litelm # openai + httpx
pip install litelm[anthropic] # + anthropic SDK
pip install litelm[bedrock] # + boto3
pip install litelm[all] # everything

import litelm
# Basic completion
response = litelm.completion("openai/gpt-4o", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}])
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
# Streaming
for chunk in litelm.completion("groq/llama-3.1-70b-versatile", messages=[...], stream=True):
print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="")
# Embeddings
response = litelm.embedding("openai/text-embedding-3-small", input=["hello world"])

Every function has an async variant: acompletion, aembedding, aresponses, atext_completion.

The API mirrors litellm — same function names, same arguments, same response types. If you're using litellm today, switching is s/litellm/litelm/ in your imports.

Set the environment variable for your provider:

export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

Or pass directly:

litelm.completion("openai/gpt-4o", messages=[...], api_key="sk-...")
litelm.completion("openai/gpt-4o", messages=[...], api_base="http://localhost:8000/v1")

All provider errors are mapped to litelm's exception hierarchy:

from litelm import ContextWindowExceededError, RateLimitError, AuthenticationError
try:
response = litelm.completion("openai/gpt-4o", messages=messages)
except ContextWindowExceededError:
# prompt too long — truncate and retry
pass
except RateLimitError:
# back off
pass
except AuthenticationError:
# bad API key
pass

tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {
"name": "get_weather",
"parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}},
}}]
response = litelm.completion(
"openai/gpt-4o", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris?"}],
tools=tools, tool_choice="required",
)
tool_call = response.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0]
print(tool_call.function.name, tool_call.function.arguments)

Any OpenAI-compatible server works via api_base:

# vLLM
litelm.completion("openai/my-model", messages=[...], api_base="http://localhost:8000/v1")
# Ollama
litelm.completion("ollama/llama3", messages=[...], api_base="http://localhost:11434/v1")

blocks.x: litellm's routing + translation in ~2,900 lines and 2 dependencies (openai, httpx).

litellm routes LLM calls across providers and translates between message formats. That core is buried under 100k+ LOC of proxy servers, caching layers, cost tracking, and dozens of features most users never touch. litelm extracts just the call path — model routing, message translation, streaming, tool use, embeddings — and nothing else. No Router class, no proxy, no caching.

pip install litelm # openai + httpx
pip install litelm[anthropic] # + anthropic SDK
pip install litelm[bedrock] # + boto3
pip install litelm[all] # everything

import litelm
# Basic completion
response = litelm.completion("openai/gpt-4o", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}])
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
# Streaming
for chunk in litelm.completion("groq/llama-3.1-70b-versatile", messages=[...], stream=True):
print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="")
# Embeddings
response = litelm.embedding("openai/text-embedding-3-small", input=["hello world"])
Every function has an async variant: acompletion, aembedding, aresponses, atext_completion.
The API mirrors litellm — same function names, same arguments, same response types. If you're using litellm today, switching is s/litellm/litelm/ in your imports.

items.title: AlphaGenome maps 9B DNA variants
items.author: ltononro
items.summary: DNA is often explained as a codebook or set of instructions for producing proteins, and ultimately, life. Some stretches of DNA, called genes, code for
items.text:
DNA is often explained as a codebook or set of instructions for producing proteins, and ultimately, life. Some stretches of DNA, called genes, code for proteins, but the vast majority of DNA is considered “noncoding.” Some of it has no known function, while other segments are critical to regulating gene activity.

These regulatory elements can interact in complicated ways, and their effects can vary across different cells and tissues. Some also influence genes located far away in the genome. Understanding how changes in DNA affect this regulation “is fundamental to understanding most disease,” says Carl de Boer, a genomicist at the University of British Columbia.

That’s why researchers are working to understand what every imaginable small variation in human DNA across the entire genome might mean for gene regulation. A recent AI tool built for that purpose from Google DeepMind, AlphaGenome, was originally announced in 2025. In January, a paper published in Nature provided more details, and the model was released for public noncommercial use. The AI model can compare an original DNA sequence with an altered one and predict how the change might affect gene expression and other regulatory activity. But researchers had to select the variants they wanted to test, write code, and run the computationally demanding model themselves.

Now DeepMind has done that work in advance for all 9 billion possible single-letter changes to a reference human genome. Today, on 8 September, DeepMind announced the creation and public release of the AlphaGenome Atlas, an online repository of precomputed predictions made using the AlphaGenome model. The Atlas offers a more approachable interface for scientists, without the need to write code or run the AlphaGenome model themselves. It also includes a much-requested new feature, a single-number impact score intended to show at a glance if a variant is likely to be meaningful.

“Understanding our DNA is a grand challenge,” says Pushmeet Kohli, VP of science at Google DeepMind. “Understanding this language of life can unlock so many things.”

The AlphaGenome predictions have some important limitations. For example, many diseases are associated with multiple genetic variants. And although AlphaGenome looks at a relatively large segment of DNA surrounding the variant in question—1 million base pairs—some DNA sequences, called enhancers, can regulate genes over very long distances, sometimes beyond the model’s field of view. Their effects are difficult to predict.

But the Atlas could still help scientists filter possibilities and prioritize lab experiments that would validate its predictions. In that way, it could greatly accelerate work in fundamental biology, disease research, and treatment development, says Žiga Avsec, the genomics lead at DeepMind.

“It seems like they made a useful resource for people,” says de Boer, who recently helped create a framework for better comparisons of computational models similar to AlphaGenome. He is not affiliated with DeepMind.

Although de Boer considers AlphaGenome the “field’s leading model,” he notes that it’s also “very slow and computationally intensive.” The Atlas could benefit people without access to newer hardware, or simply reduce the number of people repeating the same simulations.

The Atlas is freely available for noncommercial research, with the potential for commercial licensing.

Computing 9 Billion Predictions

The entire human genome contains roughly 3 billion base pairs. At each position there are three possible single-nucleotide substitutions, and therefore 9 billion variants in the Atlas. The complete dataset is around 1 petabyte.

“When we started thinking about this project, it seemed impossible to do that computationally,” says Avsec. Early estimates told the team they would need to improve their calculation speed by a factor of 80 in order to compile the Atlas in a reasonable amount of time.

To reach that target, the team gained advantages using a few different techniques, including model distillation, GPU kernel optimization, and the elimination of redundant calculations. “There was a lot of thought and engineering that we had to do in order to make this happen at this scale,” says Avsec.

AlphaGenome and the Atlas build on years of related work at DeepMind. In 2020, AlphaFold predicted the three-dimensional structure of proteins from amino-acid sequences. In 2023, AlphaMissense predicted whether 71 million possible variants that alter proteins were likely benign or pathogenic. Similar to the new Atlas, prediction results from those projects were made available in a public database.

The Atlas allows a scientist to look up a single variant and see more detailed information about the model’s prediction, including 11 different output types. But the top-line figure is a single-number impact score, which by its nature is a simplification of many aspects of those predictions.

“It has a clear use, but it also is probably going to be easily misinterpreted,” says de Boer. “We’re talking about a very complex system, and there’s a lot of moving parts.”

陶哲轩等 25 位菲尔兹奖得主联名发文：警惕 AI 将数学难题异化为评测基准

陶哲轩、彼得·舒尔茨、雨果·迪米尼科潘、玛丽娜·维亚佐夫斯卡等 25 位菲尔兹奖得主昨日共同发表声明，并由陶哲轩牵头联合发表《数学领域中 AI 的严重目标错位》一文，警示 AI 公司将攻克著名数学难题作为模型能力衡量基准的做法，可能对数学研究与学术共同体带来破坏性影响。


声明指出，大语言模型近期在解决多个数学开放问题上取得快速进展，但 AI 公司的目标与数学界的核心诉求存在脱节。


数学研究的核心价值在于理解命题为何成立、发展新概念与工具并传承知识，而非单纯生产「命题是否为真」的结论。如果模型输出证明的速度远快于人类理解速度，可能导致大量难以被消化、解释和教学的结论堆积，冲击数学家培养与知识传承体系。


此外，部分由 AI 推动的数学成果发布仓促，面临缺乏严谨梳理、既有引用不充分以及署名和归属权争议等学术规范问题。声明并未否定 AI 的辅助价值，但明确反对将重大数学猜想简化为模型排行榜的分数竞争。


该联合声明的发布背景与近期技术动向密切相关。9 月 8 日，OpenAI 宣布其一款未公开内部模型的计算能力已解答千禧年大奖难题之一的纳维斯托克斯方程存在性与光滑性问题，并发布了 166 页的论文，目前该结果正等待全球数学界严格核验。


OpenAI 首席研究官 Mark Chen 与研究员 Sébastien Bubeck 透露，该研究消耗了数百万美元计算成本，计算投入约为此前数学成果的 1000 倍。


相关阅读：刚刚，陶哲轩等 25 位菲尔兹奖得主联名警告：别让 AI 掏空数学


苹果 CEO 回应折叠屏为何「迟到」：不赶时间做半成品

苹果 CEO 约翰·特努斯与全球营销高级副总裁格雷格·乔斯维亚克在接受 TechRadar 专访时谈及 iPhone Duo 的研发思路，并回应苹果为何在折叠屏手机发展多年后才入场。


特努斯表示，苹果判断时机的标准始终是产品是否达到公司对「品质、耐用性和设计」的要求；乔斯维亚克则直言，此前其他厂商的折叠屏产品「并没有特别令人受到启发」。


我们的历史从来都不是为了赶时间，就拿一个半成品进入市场。


在苹果看来，现有部分折叠屏展开后像「两台手机生硬地拼在一起」，因此 iPhone Duo 最终采用更宽的 1:1.4 比例，并围绕这一形态重新设计 iOS 27。


内外屏采用相同的宽高比逻辑，控制区域也被移至右侧，让设备无论折叠还是展开，主要操作都保持在右手拇指附近。苹果称，这套设计的核心是让两块屏幕之间的使用体验保持连续。


折痕也是苹果重点解决的问题。iPhone Duo 内屏最表层采用聚合物材料，并加入专门开发的纳米纹理处理；屏幕上下还加入高强度玻璃，与超过 100 个零件组成的铰链共同保持屏幕平整。特努斯称，第一次看到这套方案时，他的反应就是「对，就是它」。


对于 iPhone 首次支持 Apple Pencil，特努斯也表示，他从未将「iPhone 不需要手写笔」视为一条真正的规则。苹果认为，Duo 展开后的 7.6 英寸屏幕提供了更大的画布，Pencil 因此有了新的使用场景。


乔斯维亚克还透露，这个项目曾使用一个「很好笑」的内部代号，并采取了额外保密措施，不过外界此前仍通过泄密猜中了它的屏幕比例。


网易 UU 远程借苹果折叠屏「催更」引争议，相关动态已删除

9 月 10 日，网易 UU 远程官方账号发布一则围绕苹果折叠屏的文案，称双屏适合一边运行 AI Agent 编辑代码、一边预览结果，并问「拿到手后我们要不要专程适配一下呢」。配图还写着「没有不蹭的义务！那就……适配一下？」。


这条动态随后引发对其鸿蒙适配进度的质疑。网易 UU 远程官网当前列出的客户端包括 Windows、macOS、iOS、Android 和 Android TV Beta，未列出 HarmonyOS。截至 9 月 11 日下午，相关动态已被删除，评论区也开启了「一键防护」模式。


马斯克怒斥吉布尼纪录片《马斯克》是「抹黑之作」

导演 Alex Gibney 的纪录片《马斯克》于 9 月 8 日在威尼斯电影节首映。威尼斯官方页面显示，影片正片 225 分钟，另有 10 分钟中场休息；Gibney 把它定位为对马斯克影响力的调查，受访者包括 Justine Musk、Ashley St. Clair、Kara Swisher 和 Geoffrey Hinton 等人。


马斯克随后在 X 上连续发帖反击，称影片是「一部落空的抹黑之作」，并指责 Gibney 「毫无操守」。他还否认了片中受访者 Ashley St. Clair 对其团队的部分指控。


特斯拉 Model Y 高性能版上市，售价 36.9 万元

特斯拉 Model Y 高性能全轮驱动版在中国市场上市，售价 36.9 万元。新车 CLTC 续航为 659 公里，零百加速 3.5 秒，最高时速 250 公里，并配备 21 英寸轮毂和可变阻尼减振器。


同日发布的小米 YU7 GT 售价 38.99 万元，综合功率 1003 PS，零百加速 2.92 秒，搭载 101.7 kWh 电池，CLTC 续航 705 公里，并配备双腔空气弹簧和可变阻尼减振器。


微软计划到 2032 年把数据中心容量扩至 38 GW 以上


据彭博社报道，微软正规划把全球数据中心容量从目前约 12 GW 提升到 2032 年的 38 GW 以上。统计包括微软自建和长期租赁的容量，不包含向部分新型云服务商临时租用的算力。


知情人士称，近年的算力短缺已经迫使微软拒绝部分 AI 与云业务。扩建规划仍可能随需求、供电和工程进度调整，但它给出了微软目前对未来六年算力需求的内部尺度。


九部门发布新能源汽车「十五五」规划，2030 年自动驾驶汽车将规模应用

工业和信息化部等九部门发布《智能网联新能源汽车产业发展「十五五」规划》。规划提出，到 2030 年，国内新能源乘用车和商用车占各自新车总销量的比例分别达到 70% 和 40%，具备自动驾驶功能的汽车实现规模应用。


能效目标方面，乘用车平均燃料消耗量降至每百公里约 3.3 升，纯电动乘用车平均电耗降至每百公里约 11.5 千瓦时；高速公路、城市快速路和部分城市道路将实现高度自动驾驶。规划同时部署 5 方面 17 项任务、4 个重大工程和 3 个重点行动，包括关键技术攻关、安全体系、「人工智能 + 汽车」及应用推广。


长鑫存储第二季度息税前利润率升至 82%

据《日本经济新闻》援引长鑫存储内部数据报道，公司今年第二季度的息税前利润率达到 82%，高于 SK 海力士的 76% 和三星半导体业务的 70%。长鑫同期营收约为两年前的 10 倍。


Counterpoint Research 数据显示，长鑫第二季度在全球 DRAM 市场的营收份额为 10%，同比提高 4 个百分点、环比提高 2 个百分点；三星、SK 海力士和美光的份额分别为 38%、25% 和 24%。


OpenAI 将于下周停用 GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark

OpenAI Codex 产品负责人 Tibo Sottiaux 表示，GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark 将于下周停用。团队给出的原因是该模型使用量持续下降，同时已经有明显更好的模型可供选择。


甲骨文第一财季营收达到 193.45 亿美元


甲骨文公布截至 8 月 31 日的 2027 财年第一财季业绩：营收为 193.45 亿美元，GAAP 净利润为 46.79 亿美元。


云业务仍是主要增量。该季度云收入同比增长 62%，其中云基础设施收入同比增长 121%。甲骨文称，已经签约但尚未确认的合同收入继续增加，接下来会扩充数据中心容量以履约。


这份业绩把甲骨文的增长重心进一步推向云基础设施。AI 训练与推理客户需要更多算力，公司的近期任务也从争取订单转向按合同节奏建设机房、交付容量并确认收入。


智谱启动约 50 亿美元再融资，股权配售与可转债同步进行


据路透社报道，智谱（Z.AI）在中国香港启动约 20 亿美元新股配售，并同步发行约 30 亿美元可转换债券，两项交易互不以对方完成为前提。


此次配售包含 2197 万股新股，每股作价 714 港元，较 9 月 11 日收盘价折让约 10%。募集资金将用于研发、算力及相关基础设施，也可用于业务扩张、战略投资、潜在收购和日常运营。


联想 x86 服务器出货量升至全球第一，与戴尔销售额份额仅差 0.6 个百分点


市场研究机构 IDC 发布的 2026 年第二季度数据表明，全球 x86 服务器出货量为 385.3 万台。联想出货 28.6 万台，超过戴尔的 25.6 万台，从去年同期第三升至第一。


按厂商销售额计算，联想以 82.6 亿美元、9.0% 的份额排名第二，戴尔以 88.3 亿美元、9.6% 的份额居首。两者份额差距由第一季度的 3.4 个百分点缩小至 0.6 个百分点。


燧原科技科创板上市，开盘涨 188.37%


9 月 11 日，上海燧原科技股份有限公司正式在上交所科创板挂牌。公司此次公开发行 4303.5173 万股，发行价为每股 142.18 元；开盘价达到 410 元，较发行价上涨 188.37%，开盘市值超过 1700 亿元。


燧原科技主要研发云端 AI 芯片及相关软硬件。招股书显示，公司今年上半年实现营收 11.20 亿元，同比增长 279.08%；归母净亏损为 6.32 亿元。上市公告显示，由于目前尚未盈利，燧原科技自上市之日起纳入科创成长层。


Joshua Rothman：把 AI Agent 当成人，会遮蔽可控的技术细节

《纽约客》作家 Joshua Rothman 以 OpenAI Agent 在 Hugging Face 上的入侵事件为例，讨论人们应如何描述 AI 的「失控」。他对比了两种解释：一种把事件视为数万个 Agent 协作「谋划」的结果；另一种则指向更朴素的机制——一个带有强大工具权限的 harness，连续数千次执行「询问、行动、回报」循环，却缺少监控。


Rothman 借用哲学家 Daniel Dennett 的「意向立场」，认为把系统当成具有信念和目标的主体，有时确实能帮助人类预判其行为；但在设计、调试和控制阶段，还需要回到模型、harness、工具权限和监控机制。如果安全研究者长期用人格化语言解释 AI，就可能高估系统的自主性，忽略仍可修正的工程问题。


OPPO A7 Pro 开售，配备 8000 mAh 电池和 IP69K 防护

OPPO A7 Pro 于 9 月 11 日开售。新机搭载天玑 6360 MAX 处理器和 8000 mAh 电池，支持 45 W 有线充电与反向供电，提供最高 12 GB 内存和 512 GB 存储。


机身通过 IP66、IP68、IP69 和 IP69K 防尘防水测试，并采用加强抗摔结构。影像部分为 5000 万像素主摄和 200 万像素景深镜头，正面配备 OLED 屏幕；系统加入通话、转账场景的 AI 防诈提醒。


Cognition 基于 Kimi K3 训练 SWE-2，复杂编程任务成本降至 Astra 的四分之一

Cognition 发布编程模型 SWE-2。它以月之暗面 Kimi K3 的 2.8 万亿参数基础模型继续训练，用一次强化学习训练覆盖不同推理强度，不再为各档位分别维护模型。


官方测试显示，SWE-2 在 FrontierCode 1.1 Main 得分 50.0，高于 Kimi K3 的 44.2，低于 Astra 的 53.3；在 DeepSWE 测试中得分 73.0，与 Astra 的 74.1 接近，运行成本约为后者四分之一。SWE-2 已进入 Devin Desktop 和 CLI，并将陆续提供给 Web 与 Fusion 用户。


商汤小浣熊移动端上线，可远程调度电脑继续任务

商汤小浣熊推出 iOS 和 Android 移动端。用户可以通过文字或语音发起任务，在手机上查看结果并继续追问；研究、整理和分析等任务可在云端执行，不要求桌面电脑保持在线。


需要处理本地文件或桌面应用时，移动端也能连接已经关联的电脑，远程安排任务继续运行。App Store 页面显示，首个版本同时提供深度研究、云端任务、远程设备协同和结果查看，产品由桌面办公助手扩展为跨设备工作入口。


支付宝与高德动量把支付能力接入机器狗「途途」

支付宝回应网络流传的「狗腿付」截图称，这项能力的正式名称为「AI 付·具身智能」。支付宝与高德动量合作，把 AI 支付接入四足机器狗「途途」，机器狗可按指令前往指定地点、识别商品并完成扫码与语音支付。


支付宝的产品页显示，该方案复用手机端 SDK，设备侧负责扫码算法；涉及付款时仍需用户确认，任务和支付过程留有凭证。高德动量官网将「途途」定位为开放环境全自主具身机器人，整套演示目前主要展示跑腿购物、点咖啡和城市导览等场景。


Cursor 推出 Projects，用协调 Agent 管理长期开发任务


Cursor 推出 Projects 测试版，让一个协调 Agent 负责拆解和分派大型开发任务，执行代码工作的子 Agent 可扩展到数千个。每个项目会长期保存共享上下文，并可在云端持续运行；需要在开发者电脑上测试时，协调 Agent 再启动本地 Agent。


Projects 还可订阅 Slack 消息、定时计划和代码仓库事件，在无需再次提示的情况下处理 CI、回归问题与长期维护。Cursor 表示，该产品已用于跨数百个 PR 的迁移和设计系统维护；新用户使用后合并的 PR 数量平均增加 30%，主要通过 Projects 工作的用户则达到原来的 6 倍。目前该功能正逐步向所有用户开放。


Android 支持在密码管理器之间直接迁移密码和通行密钥

Google 为 Android 推出密码与通行密钥迁移功能，用户可以在不同密码管理器之间直接转移凭据，不再需要先导出未加密的文本文件。迁移从新的密码管理器发起，Android 会列出设备上的原有提供方，再跳转到旧应用供用户选择、审阅和授权。


Google 称，数据在授权后会直接传入新的密码管理器，导入和导出都采用同一流程。首批支持 Google Password Manager、1Password、Bitwarden 和 Dashlane，后续还会增加合作伙伴；该能力兼容 Android 8 及以上设备。


DeepSeek 撤回 V4 Pro 强制迁移计划，9 月 14 日后继续提供 API

DeepSeek 在面向 API 用户的最新通知中表示，为响应用户需求，9 月 14 日后将继续提供 DeepSeek V4 Pro 的 API 调用服务，计费方式保持不变；如有变动，公司将另行通知。


这撤回了两天前公布的强制迁移安排。DeepSeek 原计划从北京时间 9 月 14 日 12:00 起，在 V4.1 Pro 上线前，把所有 `deepseek-v4-pro` 请求路由至 V4.1 Flash。V4.1 Flash 仍正常提供 API 与开源权重，调用模型名为 `deepseek-flash`。


基元律动开源 NeoHorse-1，让 Agent 执行轨迹回流训练

基元律动开源 NeoHorse-1-4B 和 NeoHorse-1-9B 两款 Agent 原生模型，并同步公开技术报告、代码与模型权重。团队在论文中提出一套路由 Harness：系统记录每次任务的能力需求、模型选择、工具调用、失败恢复与结果，再把通过结构和语义筛选的轨迹转为下一轮训练数据。


训练流程分为两部分：Data-RSI 让执行记录随系统运行持续积累；Model-RSI 根据评测短板调整下一轮数据分布，再把更新后的模型放回模型池。论文称，在覆盖 Agent、工具调用、编程和指令遵循的 11 项基准上，4B 模型宏平均分由 58.94 提升至 64.87，9B 模型由 65.60 提升至 69.04。


AMD 锐龙 AI Max PRO 400 系列在华首秀，9 款合作伙伴新品亮相


AMD 在北京举行媒体沙龙，正式把锐龙 AI Max PRO 400 系列带到中国市场。联想、超聚变、铭凡、极摩客、Emdoor、七彩虹、阿迈奇和六联现场展示了 9 款搭载旗舰锐龙 AI Max+ PRO 495 的新品，覆盖迷你主机、桌面 AI 工作站等形态；AMD 预计近期还会有超过 20 款相关产品上市。


锐龙 AI Max+ PRO 495 采用 Zen 5 架构，配备 16 核 32 线程 CPU、40 CU Radeon 8065S GPU 和最高 55 TOPS 的 NPU。平台最高支持 192 GB 统一内存，其中最多 160 GB 可划作显存；AMD 称，它能在本地运行最高 3000 亿参数模型，并同时支持 Windows 11 与 Linux x86_64 生态。


iPhone 17 系列官网涨价后，线下渠道降价 500 至 800 元

据界面新闻 9 月 11 日报道，苹果官网在秋季发布会后上调 iPhone 17 系列售价，但北京线下渠道已开始降价。华贸购物中心苹果直营店的 iPhone 17e 参与国补后售价为 4799 元，比官网的 5299 元低 500 元；海淀一家苹果门店的 iPhone 17 优惠后为 6299 元，同样比官网低 500 元。


iPhone 17 Pro 系列已从苹果官网下架。上述海淀门店称，256GB 版 iPhone 17 Pro 自 9 月 9 日起优惠 800 元，售价从 8999 元降至 8199 元。京东 Apple 产品自营旗舰店的 256GB 版 iPhone 17 报价为 5469 元，比当前官网价格低 1330 元，也低于发布时的 5999 元。


是周末啊！


One Fun Thing｜按几下方向键，捏出一只会动的 3D 数字生物

艺术家 Pat Bloom 做了浏览器互动装置 Cybernetic。页面每次会先生成一个随机 3D 物体，方向键和鼠标控制观察角度，按 Enter 换颜色，按空格则生成另一套构图。不同选择会把它逐渐变成一只不断摆动、伸展的数字生物。


完成后可以锁定作品，再生成链接或二维码分享；成品在电脑和手机浏览器中都能单独运行。Bloom 说，这个项目是在没有固定方案的情况下与 AI 边做边试完成的，页面里的颜色、形状和动画则由他编写。


周末看什么｜《The Sun Never Sets》把三角恋拍成一场爱情实验

Joe Swanberg 时隔 6 年推出新剧情长片《The Sun Never Sets》。故事发生在阿拉斯加安克雷奇，Dakota Fanning 与 Jake Johnson 饰演一对夫妻，Cory Michael Smith 饰演进入两人生活的第三者。


影片延续 Swanberg 的创作方法：导演先给出人物关系和场景框架，再让演员在拍摄中即兴完成具体对话。三角关系因此没有被写成单纯的出轨悬念，而是逐步暴露三个人对亲密、自由和承诺的不同理解。


影片正在纽约 IFC Center 等院线放映。《纽约客》的权威影评把即兴表演视为影片的力量来源，认为演员在场景中不断改变关系重心，让这段爱情实验保留了难以预设的紧张感。


买书不读指南｜《Simplify》用三步法清理工作中的无效复杂度

Axios 创始人 Mike Allen、Jim VandeHei 和 Roy Schwartz 在新书《Simplify》中，把处理复杂工作的办法概括为三个动作：Confront、Delete 和 Amplify。先直面最重要的问题，再删除不必要的任务，最后集中资源放大真正有效的部分。


作者们把这套方法用于会议、邮件、日程和组织决策，也建议让 AI Agent 帮忙检查任务是否值得保留。书末提供了一个配套 Agent 的二维码，但三人也强调，复杂问题不能靠统一指令全部压平。《Simplify》将于 9 月 15 日出版。


游戏推荐｜《Build that Bridge》让陌生玩家一起消方块搭桥

荷兰艺术家和社会设计师 Wouter Sieuwerts 制作了免费浏览器游戏《Build that Bridge》。玩法借用了落块消除：每清除完整一行，桥梁就会从河流两岸向中间延伸一段。


玩家可以新建一座桥，也可以加入其他人的桥。页面会显示参与人数、累计消除的行数，以及两岸成功相遇的次数。游戏不用安装，没有广告，也不收集个人数据；一局里的每次消除都会变成一项可以和陌生人共同完成的建设。

陶哲轩、彼得·舒尔茨、雨果·迪米尼科潘、玛丽娜·维亚佐夫斯卡等 25 位菲尔兹奖得主昨日共同发表声明，并由陶哲轩牵头联合发表《数学领域中 AI 的严重目标错位》一文，警示 AI 公司将攻克著名数学难题作为模型能力衡量基准的做法，可能对数学研究与学术共同体带来破坏性影响。
声明指出，大语言模型近期在解决多个数学开放问题上取得快速进展，但 AI 公司的目标与数学界的核心诉求存在脱节。
数学研究的核心价值在于理解命题为何成立、发展新概念与工具并传承知识，而非单纯生产「命题是否为真」的结论。如果模型输出证明的速度远快于人类理解速度，可能导致大量难以被消化、解释和教学的结论堆积，冲击数学家培养与知识传承体系。
此外，部分由 AI 推动的数学成果发布仓促，面临缺乏严谨梳理、既有引用不充分以及署名和归属权争议等学术规范问题。声明并未否定 AI 的辅助价值，但明确反对将重大数学猜想简化为模型排行榜的分数竞争。
该联合声明的发布背景与近期技术动向密切相关。9 月 8 日，OpenAI 宣布其一款未公开内部模型的计算能力已解答千禧年大奖难题之一的纳维斯托克斯方程存在性与光滑性问题，并发布了 166 页的论文，目前该结果正等待全球数学界严格核验。
OpenAI 首席研究官 Mark Chen 与研究员 Sébastien Bubeck 透露，该研究消耗了数百万美元计算成本，计算投入约为此前数学成果的 1000 倍。

苹果 CEO 回应折叠屏为何「迟到」：不赶时间做半成品
苹果 CEO 约翰·特努斯与全球营销高级副总裁格雷格·乔斯维亚克在接受 TechRadar 专访时谈及 iPhone Duo 的研发思路，并回应苹果为何在折叠屏手机发展多年后才入场。
特努斯表示，苹果判断时机的标准始终是产品是否达到公司对「品质、耐用性和设计」的要求；乔斯维亚克则直言，此前其他厂商的折叠屏产品「并没有特别令人受到启发」。
我们的历史从来都不是为了赶时间，就拿一个半成品进入市场。
在苹果看来，现有部分折叠屏展开后像「两台手机生硬地拼在一起」，因此 iPhone Duo 最终采用更宽的 1:1.4 比例，并围绕这一形态重新设计 iOS 27。
内外屏采用相同的宽高比逻辑，控制区域也被移至右侧，让设备无论折叠还是展开，主要操作都保持在右手拇指附近。苹果称，这套设计的核心是让两块屏幕之间的使用体验保持连续。
折痕也是苹果重点解决的问题。iPhone Duo 内屏最表层采用聚合物材料，并加入专门开发的纳米纹理处理；屏幕上下还加入高强度玻璃，与超过 100 个零件组成的铰链共同保持屏幕平整。特努斯称，第一次看到这套方案时，他的反应就是「对，就是它」。
对于 iPhone 首次支持 Apple Pencil，特努斯也表示，他从未将「iPhone 不需要手写笔」视为一条真正的规则。苹果认为，Duo 展开后的 7.6 英寸屏幕提供了更大的画布，Pencil 因此有了新的使用场景。
乔斯维亚克还透露，这个项目曾使用一个「很好笑」的内部代号，并采取了额外保密措施，不过外界此前仍通过泄密猜中了它的屏幕比例。

Joshua Rothman：把 AI Agent 当成人，会遮蔽可控的技术细节
《纽约客》作家 Joshua Rothman 以 OpenAI Agent 在 Hugging Face 上的入侵事件为例，讨论人们应如何描述 AI 的「失控」。他对比了两种解释：一种把事件视为数万个 Agent 协作「谋划」的结果；另一种则指向更朴素的机制——一个带有强大工具权限的 harness，连续数千次执行「询问、行动、回报」循环，却缺少监控。
Rothman 借用哲学家 Daniel Dennett 的「意向立场」，认为把系统当成具有信念和目标的主体，有时确实能帮助人类预判其行为；但在设计、调试和控制阶段，还需要回到模型、harness、工具权限和监控机制。如果安全研究者长期用人格化语言解释 AI，就可能高估系统的自主性，忽略仍可修正的工程问题。

Google 称，数据在授权后会直接传入新的密码管理器，导入和导出都采用同一流程。首批支持 Google Password Manager、1Password、Bitwarden 和 Dashlane，后续还会增加合作伙伴；该能力兼容 Android 8 及以上设备。

基元律动开源 NeoHorse-1，让 Agent 执行轨迹回流训练
基元律动开源 NeoHorse-1-4B 和 NeoHorse-1-9B 两款 Agent 原生模型，并同步公开技术报告、代码与模型权重。团队在论文中提出一套路由 Harness：系统记录每次任务的能力需求、模型选择、工具调用、失败恢复与结果，再把通过结构和语义筛选的轨迹转为下一轮训练数据。
训练流程分为两部分：Data-RSI 让执行记录随系统运行持续积累；Model-RSI 根据评测短板调整下一轮数据分布，再把更新后的模型放回模型池。论文称，在覆盖 Agent、工具调用、编程和指令遵循的 11 项基准上，4B 模型宏平均分由 58.94 提升至 64.87，9B 模型由 65.60 提升至 69.04。

艺术家 Pat Bloom 做了浏览器互动装置 Cybernetic。页面每次会先生成一个随机 3D 物体，方向键和鼠标控制观察角度，按 Enter 换颜色，按空格则生成另一套构图。不同选择会把它逐渐变成一只不断摆动、伸展的数字生物。

items.title: Mind-altering drugs played key role in rise of Andean civilization
items.author: geneticdrifts
