items.title: The Best New Cookbooks of Fall 2026
items.author: The Bon Appétit and Epicurious Staffs
items.summary: This fall, there’s no shortage of exciting new cookbooks. Ina Garten is back with her 14th title, which is all about smart streamlining because store-bought is
items.text:
This fall, there’s no shortage of exciting new cookbooks. Ina Garten is back with her 14th title, which is all about smart streamlining because store-bought is fine. Yotam Ottolenghi is dipping back into simple cooking with a sequel to his popular 2018 title, Ottolenghi Simple. And Lucas Sin is transporting us to Hong Kong’s iconic diners. The heavy hitters came to play! Read on for more standout titles of the season (organized by release date), handpicked and cooked from by our staff.

No. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World by Meherwan Irani

After a spellbinding meal at chef Meherwan Irani’s Chai Pani in Washington, DC, and many years spent electrifying my taste buds with his Spicewalla blends, I leapt at the chance to crack open Irani’s debut cookbook. His recipes and stories in it showcase a broad perspective on Indian cuisine and a career spent championing it for American audiences. The book is a riot, saturated with rich color and food, and sprinkled with hilarious commentary like “naan pisses me off.” Recipe titles like The Obligatory Saag Paneer hint at myopic expectations for Indian menus, yet Irani still offers a compelling (unblended!) version. I made the Tandoori Chicken, which is adapted for home cooks lacking a tandoor, the hot clay oven. Irani has you roast the meat at a high temperature, then give it a stint under the broiler for wonderful char. Masala Omelet Sandos are packed with layers of aromatics like onion, green chiles, and turmeric, and topped with a gooey mesmerizing layer of American cheese. —Chris Morocco, food director

No. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World: At-Home Recipes from the Streets, Truck Stops, Villages, and Palaces of India

Bake Anything by Erin Jeanne McDowell

As the saying goes, “A good teacher explains, a superior teacher demonstrates, and a great teacher inspires.” But what happens when you do all three? Erin Jeanne McDowell, the author of the seminal The Book on Pie, is no stranger to walking readers through complex baked goods and making the recipes feel achievable. Her fourth and latest book, Bake Anything, is designed to be the “building blocks of baking.” With foundational techniques, recipes are padded out with flavor variations (she offers nine different pudding ideas), storage tips (you can freeze frosting!), and even customized yields, showcasing the wide and wondrous world of sweets and treats. The Victoria Sponge Sheet Cake I made was buxom, with an otherworldly airy crumb. —Shilpa Uskokovic, senior Test Kitchen editor

Bake Anything: Essential Recipes and Techniques to Build On for Endless Possibilities

Gather Around My Table by Kay Chun

Known for her former NYC restaurant, Share, and stellar recipe development chops, I couldn’t wait to cook through Kay Chun’s debut book, Gather Around My Table. True to its title, Chun’s ethos is simple: The best cooking is all about connection. That spirit pulses through her stories: Chun shares fond childhood memories of wrapping dumplings with her mother and grandmother and regularly eating global plates of food; she was just as likely to devour Kalbi jjim (Korean braised short ribs) as she was meatloaf. “Eating this way taught me that exciting flavor comes in many forms and often from their combination,” she writes. That sensibility shines in her recipes. Kimchi brine gives her micheladas a spicy, electric lift, and earthy kale and savory seaweed lend her risotto depth. Also: doenjang carnitas. How fun is that? —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Gather Around My Table: Simple, Flavorful Recipes from My Global Pantry

Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi

I’ve long been a fan of chef Yotam Ottoglenghi’s flavorful recipes; but on busy weeknights I simply don’t have the energy to cook dishes with lengthy ingredient lists. This is exactly why I loved his 2018 book, Ottolenghi Simple, and I was delighted to see this year’s follow-up, Ottolenghi Simple Too. Cowritten with Verena Lochmuller, with additional contributions by Milli Taylor and Tara Wigley, the book picks up where the original left off. “‘Simple’ means something different to everyone,” Ottolenghi writes in the introduction. “For some, that’s cooking dinner in half an hour. For others, it’s about a slow-cooking dish that bubbles away while they’re in the garden.” The book keeps ingredient lists low (at about 10), the techniques straightforward, and the active time minimal. In the Test Kitchen, our team couldn’t get enough of the Salmon With Apricot and Cilantro Pesto (the sauce would be just as good over chicken or steak). And the Braised Halloumi With Tomatoes and Beans has become a new weeknight go-to go for me. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

Daily Dessert by Caroline Schiff

Those lucky enough to have tasted Caroline Schiff’s creations at Gage & Tollner, where she led the pastry team, have been eagerly anticipating her second cookbook. Daily Dessert shows off what Schiff does best: injecting savory ingredients into sweets and creating desserts that are both nostalgic and unlike anything you’ve ever tasted. When I made her Sage Brown Butter Loaf in the Test Kitchen, team members marveled at the quick bread’s tender texture and herbal quintessence. Equally compelling is the way Schiff has laid out this book: There is a chapter on desserts for two (or one!), including a mini tiramisu and a single pecan blondie (served warm with butterscotch sauce). The next chapter is for desserts you “Bake Once, Snack All Week.” The flavors—and imagination—are every bit as big as her iconic hair. —Joe Sevier, senior SEO editor, cooking

Daily Dessert: Treats on Repeat

East to East by Rachel Gurjar

East to East transports you from former BA staffer Rachel Gurjar’s hometown in Mumbai all the way to New York, where she now lives and works as a chef and tastemaker. Gurjar writes from a reflective, earnest place about navigating the two cities—the significance of cultural preservation, and how cooking brought her closer to herself. This intimate storytelling sits alongside a range of recipes: traditional family ones and thoughtful riffs on American classics. I made the Indian Fried Chicken and Coconut Key Lime Pie, two dishes that encapsulate one of the things Gurjar does well: make things her own. Every culture has its own fried chicken, but this one is special; it has a garlicky spice mix, a yogurt marinade that powerfully tenderizes the meat, and a topping of fried curry leaves for a fragrant boost. The pie had an extra-tangy custard and finely grated coconut in the crust—an addition that will make you wonder why you’ve never thought to do it sooner. —Inés Anguiano, associate Test Kitchen manager

East to East: Recipes and Stories from Mumbai to New York

items.title: “Japan Must Support ICC President Akane”: LDP Lawmaker Makishima Karen
items.summary: US sanctions against the International Criminal Court’s top leaders, including President Akane Tomoko, demand a firm and unambiguous response from Tokyo,
items.text:
US sanctions against the International Criminal Court’s top leaders, including President Akane Tomoko, demand a firm and unambiguous response from Tokyo, asserts LDP lawmaker and former digital minister Makishima Karen.

An Unacceptable Move

The International Criminal Court exists to promote the rule of law worldwide and to thwart the rule of force. Japan has consistently emphasized the court’s importance. I and several Diet colleagues have regularly met with ICC President Akane Tomoko to exchange views whenever she returns to Japan. She has long voiced concerns about becoming a target of sanctions, which finally came to pass with the August 18 announcement by the administration of US President Donald Trump. This is unacceptable.

On the morning of August 19, Japan time, I posted on X that we cannot turn a blind eye to this move. I also said that undermining the court’s independence poses a grave problem for the international community. Many of the comments I received echoed the view that the ICC must not be dismantled—as the Trump administration has threatened—and that we should do more to back President Akane. I believe that a large share of Japanese society supports my sentiments.

Some people ask if we are defending her simply because she is Japanese. But the ICC president should be defended regardless of nationality. That said, the government has a policy goal of increasing the number of Japanese nationals serving in senior positions at international organizations. If, after supporting their candidacies, we fail to stand by them when an ally imposes sanctions, who will aspire to leadership roles in the future? This is a key matter of diplomatic strategy.

ICC President Akane Tomoko, designated for sanctions by the Trump administration, speaks at an online press conference organized by the Japan National Press Club on August 26, 2026. (© Kyōdō)

Security Must Not Come at the Expense of the Rule of Law

Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae initially responded to the situation on August 19 by saying zannen ni omou—a phrasing that, especially once rendered in English as “unfortunate,” was criticized as overly restrained. But her subsequent statement on August 25, declaring that the measures taken by the United States are not compatible with Japan’s position, has softened such criticism. Needless to say, the alliance with the United States forms the cornerstone of Japan’s national security, but security must not come at the expense of the rule of law. You cannot trade one off for the other. Even between allies, there are times when one must speak plainly.

Some of the arguments being advanced to justify the US sanctions—such as concerns that the court could arrest US service personnel—are misleading and untenable. The United States has its own court-martial system and a functioning judiciary. The ICC does not threaten US sovereignty but plays only a complementary role. If misconceptions are spreading due to a lack of understanding, Japan needs to work with other member countries to provide clearer explanations.

Foreign and security policy matters often turn into political flashpoints in the United States, especially when elections are looming. Japan needs to factor that dynamic into its analysis, gathering information with this firmly in mind. Europe, for its part, is making a concerted effort to sustain the ICC as an institution.

The ICC is headquartered in The Hague, and the Dutch government has already taken steps to ensure that President Akane can live and work safely there. On August 26, I visited the Dutch embassy in Tokyo with Diet member Ide Yōsei to express our appreciation to Ambassador Gilles Beschoor Plug and to confirm our continued close coordination.

A Common Topic on Entrance Exams

On a visit to the Netherlands prior to the latest sanctions, I learned that ICC judges can face difficulty traveling, since they risk being detained when transiting through nonmember states critical of the court. The sanctions mean that President Akane can no longer enter the United States or attend the UN General Assembly. Even when returning to Japan, she may need to board direct flights from the Netherlands without a stopover.

Quite coincidentally, the rule of law was the theme of this year’s international politics and diplomacy essay contest organized annually by the LDP’s International Bureau. Held before the sanctions, the contest attracted submissions from a broad spectrum of the public—students from junior high school up through graduate school, as well as working adults. An essay by one high school student noted that the presidents of both the ICC and the International Court of Justice are currently Japanese. During a meeting with award recipients on July 15, I asked why the theme interested him. I was surprised to learn that the topic commonly appears on entrance exams for many competitive private high schools.

The sanctions against President Akane have been widely reported in Japan. One silver lining of the uproar may be that it has deepened public understanding of the rule of law’s critical importance to Japan’s national interest.

(Originally published on August 28, 2026, in Japanese based on an interview by Koga Kō of Nippon.com. Banner photo: Makishima Karen. © Nomura Kazuyuki.)

items.title: Actually, Dining Side-by-Side in Restaurants Is Good
items.summary:
The side-by-side dining nooks at Cynthia. Credit: Kodi Najm | Kodi Najm

All this week, the Eater Today newsletter is dedicated to editor Hot Takes, a way to
items.text:
The side-by-side dining nooks at Cynthia. Credit: Kodi Najm | Kodi Najm

All this week, the Eater Today newsletter is dedicated to editor Hot Takes, a way to release the pressure valve of crankiness that comes with sweating your way through the end of summer. This story was previously published as part of that series. Subscribe to Eater Today to see more of our editors’ boldest opinions about dining culture writ large.

I love the unspoken rules around dining out; admittedly, even more so when they make me feel like I’m earning a gold star for good decorum. I like dressing up for the occasion; I like waiting obediently at the host stand (See? I’m not pushy like other diners); and I enjoy the martyrdom role of reorganizing the table’s contents as the meal unfolds (distributing food if we’re sharing small plates, consolidating finished plates, pouring carafes).

My adherence to a certain kind of behavior around the rituals of dining, however, goes out the window when it comes to seating. Specifically, when the option arises for one kind of seating arrangement that’s usually deemed corny: dining side by side.

“Oh, so you’re side-by-side people” a server at a cocktail bar recently remarked when my partner and I opted to sit not across from each other, but next to each other at our table. Maybe the observation was harmless enough, but it scratched at the unspoken shame around the act of sitting next to your dining companion, whether romantic or platonic. Naysayers may call it cringe, or perhaps even codependent dining — a perceived act of PDA, one or two tiers short of fully making out at the bar (which — surprise! — I am also a fan of).

To the haters, I’d ask: Haven’t you ever given in to the corniness of love? And not just love with a person, but with the liberating idea that maybe you shouldn’t care what other people think (or how they sit, for that matter), really, and that you deserve to imbue the most routine of dinners with the same romantic energy as a couple feeding each other spaghetti alle vongole on a beach in Positano?

I recently had the pleasure of checking out Cynthia, a seasonal tasting-menu restaurant in New York City’s West Village, where I was seated at a side-by-side table with my Eater colleague Nadia Chaudhury. The settee was plush, the couch and table just big enough for two, and chic curtains were suspended from the ceiling to half-obscure the sides of the table for even more privacy. “My partner and I try to sit side by side in any restaurant we can,” Cynthia’s founder and general manager told me by email about the design choice, “so it was really a merge of the constraints of the space, while also trying to build the perfect table that I would want to sit at […] for those unique little cubbies [in the restaurant’s layout].”

To my surprise, a good number of my own colleagues also stood up for side-by-side dining when I surfaced the topic in Slack (“Is it really that corny?”). We talked about how nice it is to actually be able to hear your friend in a loud restaurant without shouting. Eater editor-in-chief Stephanie Wu also brought up the fact that your dining companion (meaning: their H&R Block 2009 Team Building Picnic T-shirt) also won’t be in the background of any food pictures, if you’re sitting next to each other and are the type to document each dish.

Somewhere in all of this, I’m convinced that the steely, buttoned-up pilgrim roots of this country are to blame for the side-by-side shame, because this certainly isn’t as big of a taboo for the French, for example. When I sit next to my friend or partner at a restaurant, I am no longer a one-woman island of propriety. I feel more like part of a team, like the two old man Muppets that serve as the Greek chorus for every Muppet movie. I’m having dinner, but most of all, I’m in cahoots. And isn’t that better?

In the words of Coolio, “Life is too short to not have fun; we are only here for a short time compared to the sun and the moon and all that.”

To the haters, I’d ask: Haven’t you ever given in to the corniness of love? And not just love with a person, but with the liberating idea that maybe you shouldn’t care what other people think (or how they sit, for that matter), really, and that you deserve to imbue the most routine of dinners with the same romantic energy as a couple feeding each other spaghetti alle vongole on a beach in Positano?

I recently had the pleasure of checking out Cynthia, a seasonal tasting-menu restaurant in New York City’s West Village, where I was seated at a side-by-side table with my Eater colleague Nadia Chaudhury. The settee was plush, the couch and table just big enough for two, and chic curtains were suspended from the ceiling to half-obscure the sides of the table for even more privacy. “My partner and I try to sit side by side in any restaurant we can,” Cynthia’s founder and general manager told me by email about the design choice, “so it was really a merge of the constraints of the space, while also trying to build the perfect table that I would want to sit at […] for those unique little cubbies [in the restaurant’s layout].”

To my surprise, a good number of my own colleagues also stood up for side-by-side dining when I surfaced the topic in Slack (“Is it really that corny?”). We talked about how nice it is to actually be able to hear your friend in a loud restaurant without shouting. Eater editor-in-chief Stephanie Wu also brought up the fact that your dining companion (meaning: their H&R Block 2009 Team Building Picnic T-shirt) also won’t be in the background of any food pictures, if you’re sitting next to each other and are the type to document each dish.

Somewhere in all of this, I’m convinced that the steely, buttoned-up pilgrim roots of this country are to blame for the side-by-side shame, because this certainly isn’t as big of a taboo for the French, for example. When I sit next to my friend or partner at a restaurant, I am no longer a one-woman island of propriety. I feel more like part of a team, like the two old man Muppets that serve as the Greek chorus for every Muppet movie. I’m having dinner, but most of all, I’m in cahoots. And isn’t that better?
In the words of Coolio, “Life is too short to not have fun; we are only here for a short time compared to the sun and the moon and all that.”

items.text:
Every time I see a meat tenderizer, I think of my mother. Specifically of the way in which she, as someone wary of emotional vulnerability yet full of affection (classic Boomer combo), decided to make Austrian pork schnitzel her love language — and the meat tenderizer her translator. In hindsight, that steel hammer was one of the best, most essential cooking tools in our home; it was also a beginner-friendly tool for me, a Montessori kid used to playing with saws at recess and expressing my feelings via dried bean art.

That tenderizer has become a staple of my kitchen ecosystem today. But one person’s tenderizer is another’s hand-me-down whisk, Japanese chef’s knife, or grill press. So what do other people consider their ride-or-die cooking tools? What are the baseline peelers, knives, and spatulas that are in constant rotation, the tools that make you feel like a culinary John Wick? I decided to ask not just chefs, but chefs with culinary school teaching experience (aka endless patience and a knowledge of novice-level skillsets) about what they consider to be the best beginner cooking tools.

In addition to a few of my own cooking essentials, I picked the brains of four teachers with experience in a variety of programs, from Hot Bread Kitchen — a New York City nonprofit that helps immigrants break into the food industry — to the legendary Institute of Culinary Education, all in the hopes of answering the inherently relative question of what constitutes an essential cooking tool for beginners.

Whether or not your new kitchen workhorse is destined to become an heirloom, some dos and don’ts for your search…

Do: Look for tools that don’t just do one thing.

Do: Read product reviews.

Don’t: Spend more than you need to on, say, a pair of tongs. And if you’re lucky enough to have a grandpa with a sick filet knife, maybe ask him about it.

First, grab a meat tenderizer.


Kitexpert Meat Tenderizer

Where to Buy:

$14.99 $11.98 at Amazon


Now, let’s talk essentials.

The best beginner cooking tools, according to Hot Bread Kitchen culinary teachers

Hot Bread Kitchen is a NYC-based culinary institute whose goal is to “uplift women, gender-expansive people, immigrants, and people of color” by helping them launch their careers in the food industry through intensive culinary training. Culinary instructors Kandy Williams and Charlene Johnson are two of the organization’s many acclaimed teachers, and they had some choice advice on the best beginner cooking tools.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hot Bread Kitchen (@hotbreadkitchen)


A great spatula

“Spatulas are often one of the first tools that I introduce to my kids to learn to use when cooking because they’re safe and easy to handle,” says Williams. “It’s your all-in-one tool — perfect for flipping, stirring, and scraping every bit of batter from a bowl.”

“I love to use a silicone spatula to gently fold ingredients like egg whites into batter,” Williams goes on. “As a baker, this is one of my favorite tools in the kitchen. I use it all the time when I prepare my buttercreams, cakes, and alfajores (Peruvian macarons). This keeps the mixture light and fluffy.”

Johnson seconds the tool’s utility for not only whipping up meals, but also allowing you to store your leftovers and ingredients. “It will allow you to get every bit of your food from containers,” she says, “to where they need to be — in your belly!”

Reach for a BPA-free silicone spatula such as this high-rated option that costs less than an order of avocado toast. It’s heat-resistant up to 600 degrees Fahrenheit, has a stainless steel internal frame — just like RoboCop — and a slightly curved blade for scraping and folding with precision.


DI ORO Silicone Spatula

Where to Buy:

$13.97 at Amazon


A workhouse vegetable peeler

At home, Williams relies on a high-quality peeler to prep everything from mashed potatoes to causa peruana with her kids; it makes prep work much faster for her students and more efficient for her as a culinary instructor. “I always show how to use a peeler safely by peeling away from the body and using short, controlled strokes. They use it to peel potatoes, carrots, butternut squash, and more vegetables. It’s also a great tool to introduce them to different textures.”

Johnson also swears by the power of the classic Swiss peeler, specifically — and not just for veggies. “It’s efficient and precise,” she says. “Use it on chocolate, cheese, or citrus. Get creative. FYI, the purpose of the protruding circle to the side of the peeler is to remove potato eyes.”

Williams Sonoma’s straight swivel-action, steel blade peeler contours to the shape of whatever potato, pear, or state fair butter sculpture you’re peeling:


Williams Sonoma Prep Tools Straight Swivel Peeler

Where to Buy:

$22.95 at Williams Sonoma


For a classic Swiss peeler, you can’t go wrong with a Victorinox straight blade, which has been GOATed by many. It’s peeler is lightweight, is made with a nonslip textured handle, and is under $10 on Amazon.


Victorinox straight-blade peeler

Where to Buy:

$9 at Amazon


A solid paring knife

As Williams says, a paring knife is “small and versatile, perfect for tasks that require precision, like peeling, trimming, or slicing small fruits and veggies.” She introduces the tool to beginner students to use for more delicate tasks — such as cutting strawberries, scoring tomatoes, or trimming herbs — in order to build their knife skills safely. “In classes my students use a paring knife to practice the concasse technique,” she says, “They love to prepare ratatouille. The paring knife is often called the ‘extension of the hand’ because it’s so maneuverable.”

Quality knives can be a costly investment, but beginners will appreciate the affordable paring knife from Quince. Its 3.5-inch paring knife is made out of 33 layers of Japanese Damascus stainless steel — which helps it achieve excellent blade balance — and it features a naturally water-resistant Pakkawood handle.


Quince Essential Japanese Damascus steel 3.5” paring knife

Where to Buy:

$39.9 at Quince


An offset serrated knife

Johnson says her serrated knife is key for cutting bread, slicing tomatoes, and more. “It’s great for anything that has a tough exterior and soft interior,” she explains. “The offset handle provides space so that the blade hits the cutting board before my hand. Efficient and delivers stellar results. 10 out of 10.”

This 9-inch offset blade sports an ergonomic handle and a serrated blade that does the job of the fancier versions at an entry-level price.


Mercer Culinary Offset Bread Knife

Where to Buy:

$27.99 at Amazon


The best beginner cooking tools, according to Celine Beitchman of the Institute of Culinary Education

The Institute of Culinary Education (ICE) was founded in 1975, and is ranked as the number-one culinary school in the United States, with locations in New York City and Los Angeles. Celine Beitchman, director of nutrition, tells me that she has been “teaching health-promoting culinary arts for about a decade,” and “became a chef over a 20-year period working in prep kitchens, restaurants, catering, and as a private chef,” first at the Natural Gourmet Institute and now within ICE’s Plant-Based Culinary Arts program.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Institute of Culinary Education (@iceculinary)


A big, sharp chef’s knife

If you don’t know where to begin with your own knife drawer, Beitchman recommends starting with an 8- to 10-inch chef’s knife. As she says, “It’s vital to handle most of the essential vegetable cuts, and for slicing everything from cheese to cake. A good knife will last, and it’s worth investing in one that you are comfortable using — one that’s not too long or heavy for you.” Check out our full guide to the best chef’s knives here, for every budget and purpose.

One of my first kitchen knives was a Made In blade, and I remember thinking, Wow, so this is what it feels like to hold a knife with its own backbone. Or, maybe what I was feeling was the single rod of stainless steel that extends from tip to handle, which is what the brand claims sets it apart. Years later, my 8-inch Made In chef’s knife still chops everything from crunchy cabbage to a tarte tatin with ease, despite my less-than-perfect knife skills.


Made In 8-inch chef’s knife

Where to Buy:

$129 $99.99 at Made In


If you’re shopping on more of a budget, I also can’t recommend Imarku’s chef’s knife enough. This 8-inch stainless steel blade cuts with as much precision as some of my friends’ fancy Wüsthof knives, but it costs under $50. I do need to sharpen it more frequently than some pricier knives (I find that the sweet spot is around every two months), but you really can’t beat the bang for your buck on this sucker. Plus, it ships in a secure, velvet-esque-lined box that makes for a thoughtful (last-minute) housewarming gift.


Imarku Japanese Chef’s Knife (8-Inch)

Where to Buy:

$39.99 at Amazon


Spring-loaded tongs

“Spring-loaded tongs with metal or rubber-coated tips can be used to toss salads in dressings or vegetables in seasonings before they hit the oven,” says Beitchman. “When I started cooking, tongs were almost an extension of my own hand and they let me reach further down the stove or up to the salamander.”

These stainless 12-inch long steel tongs come from one of my favorite affordable cookware brands, OXO. Scalloped edges are a big plus for me when it comes to tongs, because they allow for better precision and grip when I’m flipping whole padrón peppers on the grill or prodding my veggies around in a skillet. Plus, the slight concave of the tongs make it easy to ladle excess oils or sauce from a pan, (which I love to do when I’m frying eggs in chile crisp).


Oxo stainless steel tongs

Where to Buy:

$14.99 at Wayfair


Bench scraper

Finally, Beitchman stands by the power of the bench scraper. “[Bench scrapers] are amazingly versatile,” she says, “and can be used to move and lift food off of cutting boards and trays, to scrape flours and shape loaves before baking,” and more.

Crate & Barrel has gone the extra mile with this stainless steel bench scraper, which includes not only a soft-touch plastic handle that won’t slip from your grip, but a sweet little built-in ruler. It’s always a plus when a kitchen staple can combine more than one tool or function, and being able to measure out and chop your dough with one hand is a clutch time saver.


Crate & Barrel bench scraper

Where to Buy:

$19.95 at Crate & Barrel


The best beginner cooking tools, according to chef Vanessa Seder

Vanessa Seder has worked as a chef, food stylist, cookbook author, and associate food editor at Ladies’ Home Journal — to name just a handful of her culinary accomplishments — in addition to teaching for many years at the storied Stonewall Kitchen Headquarters in York, Maine. She, too, sang the praises of sharp chef’s knives and different-sized spatulas, but she also recommended a few more less-obvious tools.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Vanessa Seder (@vanessa_seder_eats)


A high-quality wood cutting board

It seems easy enough to remember, but a quality cutting board can sometimes go overlooked when you’re outfitting your kitchen with beginner cooking tools and equipment. Seder recommends John Boos & Co., one of the oldest manufacturers of butcher blocks in the country. She says that she loves the sturdy feel of her Boos board, which is 1.5 inches thick and perfect for rolling out dough while baking or making pasta, and also gives the board a bit of a height boost — a plus that she appreciates, she says, given that she’s on the taller side and doesn’t want to slouch while chopping or rolling herbs. It’s also quite a looker in terms of items that can take up precious real estate on your kitchen counters. As Seder says, “I use it sometimes as a cheese platter when we have guests over.”


John Boos Cutting Board (20” x 15”, Cherry Wood)

Where to Buy:

$158.95 at Amazon


A whetstone for sharpening knives

Those paring and chef’s knives aren’t going to sharpen themselves. As Seder says, “Learning how to sharpen your knives will save you money and time in the long run. A sharp knife is safer to use in that it prevents slippage, which can result in injury.” But getting your knives sharpened professionally can really add up in cost, she adds, so throwing down for a whetstone can be a great long-term investment. Consider this Japanese-made ceramic whetstone by King, which only costs about $50. There’s a dedicated Eater guide to sharpening your knives like a pro, but suffice to say this kit comes with everything you need: a 1000/6000 grit combination whetstone (with the former for main sharpening and the latter for finish sharpening), an angle holder for blade-sharpening accuracy, and a quick-drying cloth.


King whetstone

Where to Buy:

$52.99 at Amazon


A fish spatula

Seder says that she still has her fish spatula from culinary school, a trusty Wüsthof that continues to go the distance. This 6.5-inch slotted fish spatula from the German brand is about more than just fish, and acts as a flexible tool for cooking not only fish, but anything delicate. The Wüsthof version has earned heaps of praise for its being lightweight, angled, and slotted, which allows excess oils to drain through when you’re moving things around. Or as one reviewer writes, “Sometimes it is the small things in life that give you the motivation to be a better cook.” Our thoughts exactly.


Wüsthof slotted fish spatula

Where to Buy:

$65 at Amazon

$65 at Wüsthof


One more bonus tip: Invest in stainless steel cookware

A canon event in becoming a (slightly more) serious home cook is graduating from whatever ragtag collection of nonstick pans you’ve been accumulating since sophomore year of college to a proper set of cookware that will stand the test of time. Look in any commercial kitchen, and you’ll see stainless steel, stainless steel, stainless steel. Why? Because stainless steel cookware is durable, versatile, and has great heat conductivity and retention.

That’s why we took our collaboration with Heritage Steel seriously; our high-quality, 5-ply stainless steel pans are ready to take on any and all cooking projects, from perfect pancakes to sunny-side-up eggs to seared salmon (in which case the spatula above will come in handy). The 12-inch pan is the perfect do-everything size, while the 3-quart saucier (which also comes with a lid) can cook pasta, poach eggs, and so much more.


Eater x Heritage Steel 12-Inch Fry Pan

Where to Buy:

$129.95 at Heritage Steel

Eater x Heritage Steel 3-Quart Saucier With Lid

Where to Buy:

$169.95 at Heritage Steel

items.author: Yang-Yi Goh

items.text:
“This story is just going to be an advertisement about how GQ changes lives,” Jeremy O. Harris says, laughing over Zoom.

The acclaimed playwright is seated next to photographer-turned-filmmaker Xavier Tera in the light-drenched living room of a gilded Venetian palazzo. The pair are in town for the Venice Film Festival premiere of Tera’s feature debut, The Colour of the Sun, which Harris produced alongside Jane Chartier, Stella Savino, and Shogen. It’s the culmination of a journey that began four years ago, when Tera met Harris while shooting him in Tokyo for a GQ Japan story in 2022.

Evan Woods / Courtesy of Jeremy O Harris

“Jeremy was in Japan to release his play Daddy,” Tera recalls, “so we did that photo shoot and then just hung out for a month. We went to Fuji Rock, the Coachella of Japan, and just traveled around, and that sparked our friendship.”

Somewhere in that span, Tera mentioned an idea for a movie that he couldn’t stop thinking about, based on a book of portraits of Okinawan youth he’d shot for Marc Jacobs. “He showed me the beginnings of the script and I was like, ‘If there’s any way I can help, let me know,’” Harris says. “So part of our friendship in the years since that initial shoot were these epistolary romance writing sessions. Xavier would send me different drafts and we’d talk about it until we got to the one that we’re at now. It was amazing.”

The resulting film is a lush and sensual coming-of-age story, told in both Japanese and English, that examines the crosscultural tensions intrinsic to Okinawa—an island annexed by Japan in the late 19th century that, since World War II, has housed one of America’s biggest military installations on foreign soil. The Colour of the Sun follows two teens—one Ryukyu, the island’s indigenous culture, and an American living on the base—navigating a complicated relationship. “The backdrop is a little darker,” Tera says, “because obviously the military brings a lot of issues in Okinawa. So that creates a shadow over this friendship, where we see this generational trauma that comes and changes the perception of these two kids toward each other.”

Evan Woods / Courtesy of Jeremy O Harris

Evan Woods / Courtesy of Jeremy O Harris

A few days ahead of the premiere, Harris and Tera were spending plenty of time with their film’s young cast, some of whom had never left Okinawa before. “Our star, Naoto [Shimajiri], was standing at the airport in front of a guy who had a sign with his name on it, and he had no idea that it was for him,” Harris says. “He thought we would be there to pick him up.”

Despite that greenness, Harris and Tera had already seen flashes of readiness for the spotlight in their actors—particularly during a fitting for the Maison Margiela looks they’d all be wearing at the festival. “Once they put on the clothes, it was so cool to see how quickly they were able to ease into being movie stars,” Harris says. “There was no hesitation. It was like all of a sudden I saw Yuma [Taira] just putting her hands like this and standing on the carpet already in her head.”

Tera says that Margiela (whose team he also first met through GQ Japan) felt like the perfect choice to represent The Colour of the Sun, which was filmed entirely on 35 millimeter. “Margiela has always been so great at pushing for different textures, and the film is very much about that visually,” he says.

“A movie premiere is a moment when everyone gets to be in a band together,” Harris adds. “You want the band to all show up looking right and playing their parts properly, so you need a designer that is dynamic enough to really show off all of the different colors of the players in your band.” Unsurprisingly, when the crew hit the red carpet on Wednesday night—all glammed up in hair and make-up by Giovanni Errol—their luscious mix of velvets and tweeds and silks looked supremely rock-’n’-roll. (Today, the film was awarded the prestigious FIPRESCI International Critics Prize.)

After the premiere, Harris had planned an afterparty the likes of which La Serenissima had never seen before: a bash at the Palazzo de Fiori complete with sake cocktails, sick custom merch, and DJ sets by the film’s composers, Nosaj Thing and Jacques Greene.

“We’re throwing the craziest rager ever,” he says. “The one negative I have about the Venice Film Festival? Love it, but no one rages here. Because Venice is a very old city, and I feel like people like to go to bed early. But this is going to be a big house party rager that lasts until the wee hours.”

items.title: Do You Actually Need to Wash Your Face Twice a Day?
items.author: Michele Ross
items.summary: Even if your skincare regimen lasts no longer than 60 seconds, chances are you’ve been washing your face morning and night on autopilot for years. But unlike
items.text:
Even if your skincare regimen lasts no longer than 60 seconds, chances are you’ve been washing your face morning and night on autopilot for years. But unlike brushing your teeth twice daily, this cadence isn’t exactly gospel. While some guys could use the extra wash, others would do just fine—better, even—replacing one of those cleanses with a simple splash of water.

So which camp are you in? Your skin type has a lot to do with it—but so do your workouts, the weather, and what you slathered on your face the night before.

When a single daily cleanse will suffice

One grooming rule worth sticking to? Washing your face every night, without fail. “By the end of the day, oil, dirt, sweat, and other impurities have had time to build up on the skin, making it important to wash your face with a gentle cleanser before bed,” says Whitney Hovenic, MD, a board-certified dermatologist, Mohs surgeon, and co-founder of SPOOGE.

Your morning cleanse is more negotiable. According to Antony Nakhla, MD, a double-board certified dermatologist, dermatologic surgeon, and founder of Eighth Day, splashing your face with water is enough for those whose skin is dry or sensitive. The same goes for drama-free “normal” skin, assuming you didn’t layer on any actives (like a retinoid) before bed. “Washing skin that has nothing on it just strips the oils it needs,” he says.

Some guys are prone to overcleansing—think washing three-plus times daily, using harsh bar soaps, or using strong products (like acne washes and exfoliants) too often, all of which leave your skin worse for wear. “This strips lipids faster than skin can replace them, and the skin responds by overproducing oil or turning reactive,” says Dr. Nakhla. Your face will tell you if you need to scale things back. Revise your strategy if your skin gets red or feels tight after washing, and if it’s basically begging to be replenished with a moisturizer straight away. “If your face feels squeaky, stripped, or uncomfortable, that is usually a sign to rethink either the cleanser or how frequently you are using it,” says Dr. Hovenic.

When twice-daily cleansing is the right move

If your skin is oily, acne-prone, or you used an active ingredient the night before, Dr. Nakhla says to stick with your morning cleanse. Ditto if you’re a hot sleeper or live in a hot or humid climate, as sweat mixes with sebum to create buildup. That said, your cleansing schedule might also change with the seasons. A twice-daily cleanse might make more sense during a sweltering summer, whereas indoor heat in the wintertime can make your skin drier and render a morning refresh less necessary.

Then there are your workouts to consider. Sometimes your face-washing schedule has less to do with the clock than when you work up a sweat. If a workout leaves you drenched, you should follow up with a thorough cleanse, especially if you’re acne-prone. “Sweat itself is not ‘dirty,’ but when it sits on the skin alongside oil, sunscreen, bacteria, and debris, it can contribute to irritation and breakouts,” says Dr. Hovenic. But what if you squeeze in a run at lunch and don’t have a cleanser handy? Rinse your face at the very least. You could also consider packing a hypochlorous acid spray—which has antibacterial properties—in your gym bag or at your desk. “I would still consider it a bridge rather than a replacement for cleansing,” says Dr. Hovenic, “because a spray is not going to remove oil, sunscreen and buildup the way a cleanser can.”

How to find the right cleanser

All said, your skin’s needs, your environment, and your lifestyle will dictate whether it’s best to wash up once or twice daily. Your protocol could shift one season—or even one day—to the next. But frequency is only part of the equation. You also have to make sure you’re using the right cleanser to begin with.

Per Dr. Nakhla, guys with oily, acne-prone, or combination skin tend to do well with gel cleansers.

Prequel

Facial Gleanser Cleanser

Klur

Gentle Matter Cleanser

Skew dry or sensitive, or use retinoids at night? He recommends opting for a cream or milky cleanser, as they’re more nourishing.

Ursa Major

Making Moves Milky Cleanser

Aēsop

Gentle Facial Cleansing Milk

Exfoliating cleansers also have their place. “Use them a few times a week, not daily, and use with caution if you’re already using an acid or retinoid elsewhere,” says Dr. Nakhla. FYI: Salicylic acid is an exfoliant found in some cleansers that helps combat excess oil, clogged pores, and breakouts. However, Dr. Hovenic says you can skip the active in your face wash if you’re already using an acne treatment elsewhere in your routine.

iS Clinical

Clinical Cleansing Complex

Eighth Day

Restorative Cleanser

And it bears repeating: Lay off abrasive scrubs and toss any soaps or washes that leave your skin tight, dry, or angry. “Stronger is not automatically more effective,” says Dr. Hovenic. “The best cleanser is one that gets your skin clean without leaving your barrier paying the price.”
